speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for abandoning the Canadian Aerospace Industry through the sale of de Havilland Aircraft Ltd. to the Boeing Corporation and for its consequent failure to protect the aerospace technology paid for by Canadian taxpayers and developed by de Havilland.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is very clear from the announcement made yesterday by the Government that the present Conservative Government intends to pick up where the Diefen-baker Government left off, in terms of selling out Canada's aerospace industry. Canadian ownership ought to be a matter of vital concern in certain crucial sectors of the Canadian economy. The aerospace industry is one of those sectors.
The Canadian Government, which was determined to take us into the future, ought to be one that is putting more emphasis on Canadian ownership and Canadian control in such sectors. Instead of marching us into the future, the present Government is marching as fast as it can into the past. [Translation]
It is a sad day for the aerospace industry in this country and it is a sad day for Canada. We are selling a company in which Canadian taxpayers have invested millions of dollars, at a time when we are starting to reap the profits of our investment and should be starting to reap the benefits of sales of many Dash-7 and Dash-8 aircraft throughout the world. Thanks to the Conservatives, we are letting Boeing reap the benefits of Canadian investment. What lack of vision! What a ridiculous decision! What a typically Conservative decision!

There are two principal reasons that we in the New Democratic Party find this decision by the Conservative Government to be deeply contrary to the interests of Canada. The first of these pertains to the important matter of Canadian control in a crucial sector of our own economy. The second aspect of the decision is that even in terms of a business deal, in dollars and cents value, what the Conservatives are doing is a complete abomination. It will remind all Canadians of the incredibly inept way they made a decision last March in dealing with the
crisis in the banking industry. They are costing us millions and millions of dollars; that is the truth.
[DOT] (UIO)
I want to say something about the recent history of the de Havilland Corporation. As Canadians will know, it was originally a branch plant operation of Hawker Siddeley. During one part of its development, it indeed produced aircraft which had become known throughout the world, not simply in Canada, as a first-rate product. Of course I am referring to the Otter, the Twin Otter and the Beaver aircraft which are used not only in our own land but in many countries throughout the world. In the early 1970s, Hawker Siddeley for whatever reason-and it was not accidental that it was owned and controlled outside our borders-decided not to put the required investment into the Canadian branch plant which was necessary for the full development of the Dash-7 and other inter-urban commuter aircraft. Having made that decision, the Government of Canada was faced with the decision of having a modern industry go under or of coming in with capital to ensure proper development. At that time, the Government made the correct decision. It decided to put in what amounted to some $700 million over the years, to ensure the proper development of a modern or a series of modern first-rate aircraft.
The point I want to make about this is that this kind of capital investment makes a lot of sense in an industry of this kind. In my own small part of Canada where 1 was born, the area of Oshawa which I now have the honour to represent, the General Motors Corporation is putting in over $1 billion in the short run, in that little community alone, for a relatively few jobs to ensure longer range jobs.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: They make money too.

I will deal with the point which I just heard from the Conservative side of the House in a moment and talk about the friends of the Conservatives, the Boeing Corporation. The key point I want to make is that if we are to have development in a modern industry, we have to put up the bucks. Since the parent firm, Hawker Siddeley, was not prepared to do that, we in Canada made the proper decision to use public funds for creative investment. Now, however, just at the point when we are about to have a return on that investment, just when the company has orders on its books for its remaining production in the coming year, what does the Government decide to do? Instead of taking advantage of the productive investment which has gone on in the past decade in this industry, instead of starting to sell airplanes around the world and bringing back a return to the public of Canada for

December 3, 1985
Supply
its investment, the Government which was elected just a year ago has decided to sell it off.
It is giving it away.

I hear one of my colleagues saying: "It is giving it away". I will document that in just a moment.
The key point I want to make in this part of my argument about the nature of this kind of industry is that every country around the world involved in the aerospace industry, without exception, uses public funds. Many countries in western Europe, whether it be France, Great Britain or Japan, use public funds in the form of public participation in the industry. In fact, there are some outright ownerships by Governments.
Let us look at the United States. I hope the Minister will deal with this argument. He is making much of the cost of $700 million and how the Canadian people will not be saddled with this kind of investment, according to the Conservatives. I did some checking of the Boeing Corporation in the United States. The Government says that the Boeing Corporation is a private firm which makes its way in the market-place.
It is profitable.

One Conservative has just said: "It is profitable". There is a good reason for its being profitable. It is not the only reason, but it gets a lot of money from American taxpayers.
What corporation is at the top of the list of corporations in the United States which receive the most benefits from American taxpayers? Is it General Motors, IBM or any one of the other corporate giants outside the aerospace industry? Of course not. The company which receives the highest level of assistance from American taxpayers is none other than the Boeing Corporation. For the years 1981 and 1983, the Boeing Corporation received $400 million in the form of subsidies- and that is what they amount to-and special tax benefits from the American Government. It received $400 million in two years. At the same time it listed profits of $1.5 billion, but it did not pay one cent in income tax to the American people. That is another story about which many American citizens are concerned. The aerospace industry around the world, not just the Canadian industry, has been subsidized by taxpayers. However, there is only one Government in the modern world which is stupid enough not to recognize this necessity and is stupid enough to want to get rid of it in its own country, and that is the Conservative Government of Canada.
Hear, hear!

I ask the Minister who will be participating in this debate whether he thinks for a minute that the American people and the American Government would permit the Boeing corporation to be bought up by an enterprise or a country outside their own nation? I have just said that in two years the taxpayers of the United States put up the equivalent of $400 million Canadian for Boeing. If we look at the actual past two decades of the history of the Boeing Corporation and
the way in which it financed research and development in the aerospace industry in the United States, I know I understate the degree of subsidy when I say that it is in excess of $2 billion. That is what the Boeing Corporation has received in the past decade or so from American taxpayers.
The American flag will be very clearly waved on top of the American industry, and Americans will ensure that that happens. What is tragic is that we in Canada have a Conservative Government which, following its own past bad history of the Avro Arrow, is now taking down the Canadian flag from a Canadian corporation that is just about to take off and is wrapping itself as a Government in the Stars and Stripes. I think that is deplorable.
Shame, shame!

Is it any wonder that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be going down to Chicago tomorrow as the guest speaker of Time magazine? The next thing we know, the Prime Minister of Canada will be selected as Time magazine's man of the year.
Hear, hear!
For good reason, because he is a great Canadian.

There they are, the new Conservatives on the other side of the House, publicly cheering a Prime Minister who has just sold out one of our major industries. I say to those Conservatives: "Some sense of perspective!"
Not only is it bad for its possible implications for the long-range development of high-technology jobs in Canada, it is also, if I can put it in a way that even the Conservatives will understand, a bad business deal in terms of dollars and cents.
I want the House to consider some of the details. Ostensibly, on paper, we are supposed to be getting $155 million. That is a giveaway even at that terribly low price, but I want to study the figures and see how much we will really be getting. Of the $155 million, the poor old Boeing Corporation is being asked to put up, $90 million is as a cash down payment, and it is to pay $65 million over time. We are allowing the Boeing Corporation to buy out a crucial Canadian company on time, the way Canadians buy cars or TV sets.
When we analyse the figures, Mr. Speaker, we find something that is deeply disturbing. If Boeing makes $325 million worth of purchases in Canada over the next 15 years it will be eligible for $65 million in benefits from the Canadian Government. I see the Minister nodding. He knows very well that given the potential of the Canadian aerospace industry, which is some 40,000 strong with 100 firms in the industry, there is not the slightest doubt that Boeing can make sufficient purchases to get $65 million back.
What about the remaining $90 million? Boeing will get back an estimated $30 million of the $90 million as a result of the Government's agreement to pick up new insurance costs as
December 3, 1985

well as assuming new costs for certain future potential liabilities for faulty aircraft. The Government has reached into the taxpayers' pocket again for this $30 million which it will provide in benefits to the Boeing Corporation.
As for the remaining $60 million of the original $90 million, Boeing will simply have to invest a certain amount for increased productive capacity in Canada to write off the cost of that eventually. As the Minister no doubt knows, if Boeing invests $115 million, as it plans to do, as a result of the Government's decision Boeing will be eligible for financial assistance under the Defence Industry Productivity Program of roughly $60 million.
It is therefore very clear, Mr. Speaker, that not only are we permitting Boeing to buy out a crucial Canadian industry but, due to the ineptness of the Government, Boeing is going to be able to buy out a Canadian industry with Canadian money. What a disgrace, Mr. Speaker. It is bad enough to drink Canada dry, but it is even worse for Canadians to have to put up the money. The Government deserves to be defeated on this matter as much as it does on anything it has done since it was elected.
Hear, hear!
They call themselves businessmen.

My colleague will be adding further information which pertains to the Government's excuse for this abominable deal when he speaks.
I want to conclude very rapidly with three possible options from which the Government ought to have chosen from instead of taking the route that it has. The Government must recognize, as most other modern nations in the world that have maintained an aerospace industry have sensibly recognized, that the public sector is a very important way of doing this. The first option the Government should have seriously considered was to maintain this successful corporation, which had a $700 million investment in it, and to pursue international markets in order more rigorously pursue international markets to sell more DASH-7s and DASH-8s and other products in the future.
If the Government wanted de Havilland to have access to Boeing's international marketing network, why in heaven's name did it not go after a joint venture? Why could some deal not have been negotiated with Boeing? Boeing has negotiated deals with other countries. Why could we not have said that we will maintain this Crown corporation, we will maintain Canadian control and guarantee Canadian jobs, and have a joint arrangement with Boeing which involves some payment for access to Boeing's marketing capacity? That would have been another option which could have been exercised without losing Canadian control of this important industry.
The third option which could have been considered, if necessary, was more rigorous pursuit of a private Canadian owner. If the route of private ownership was to be chosen, a more systematic effort ought to have been made to get a Canadian owner to ensure that the industry would remain in
Supply
Canadian hands. It is certainly our clear understanding from the development position of this industry that, of all the options, it would probably have made the most sense to keep that corporation in the public sector. The public made the investment in it and ought now to be getting the benefit of that investment.
I want to conclude by observing that the Government was elected just over a year ago on the promise that it was going to take the country rapidly and more confidently into the future. In decision after decision since the Government was elected it has done just the opposite. Whatever transpires in the weeks and months ahead in terms of the Government's thinking, the New Democratic Party will remain committed to the future of the country, to the view that crucial industries ought to remain Canadian-owned, and to the view that public investment can make a lot of sense for the short run and the long run for the development of our nation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech of the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). I noticed that he said that the Boeing Corporation in the United States had received $400 million Canadian "in the form of subsidies because that's what they amount to". I think I have quoted him accurately. That is what caught my attention. I wonder if the Member could give us a breakdown of where that $400 million came from. Was it in the form of contracts or in the form of tax benefits? Could he enumerate that?

I would be very happy to get that data for the Hon. member. I can tell him that the general category is in fact all of the benefits and it is the equivalent of $400 million Canadian in the form of special tax concessions. For the Member's benefit, it came from an American source that was very critical of this use of American taxpayers' money. That aside, it was $400 million in special tax concessions, the final result of which was that Boeing, which had in excess of $1 billion in profit, ended up paying not a cent in taxes to the American Government.

Mr. Speaker, the Member said they were special tax concessions. Were they different from any other tax concessions made to any other companies? In that way does the Member view this as a special subsidy to Boeing as distinct from any other companies?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that they were not special. I have no reason to believe that they were special to Boeing. They were special only in the sense that the ordinary taxpayer in the United States, like the ordinary taxpayer in Canada, simply is not eligible for these kinds of benefits. The key point I was making is that the Americans have taken care to ensure the development in the U.S. of a world-class firm in this very modern industry. They have used the money of the American taxpayers to do so. I would suggest to the Hon. Member that Boeing has received more from the American taxpayers on a comparative basis than de Havilland has received from the Canadian taxpayers. Having put up this

December 3, 1985
Supply
money, the Americans have enough sense to make sure that the industry will remain American controlled. The key point is that the Canadian Government should have enough sense to do the same thing for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question to ask of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). It was over 20 years ago that the Conservative Government of that day, the last majority Conservative Government, decided to destroy the Avro Arrow program. I was a teenager at the time and I recall that happening. In the 20 odd years that have passed since then, most Canadians have agreed that that was a decision which destroyed the aerospace industry in Canada. We lost the research and we lost the lead that we had at that time. The situation was so bad that the Conservative Government destroyed the prototype of that particular airplane and cut it up into small pieces so that the Canadian industry could not benefit from the research for which the Canadian Government had paid.
Since this is a decision which not only affects the workers of today but the future of Canada for the next 20 or 30 years, should we not have a full discussion and committee investigation into the implications of this sale to the industry?

Mr. Speaker, the quick answer to that question will not surprise the House. What may surprise the House is the fact that I did not have advance knowledge of the question. I say that honestly. What will not surprise the House is that I agree with the thought and wisdom behind the question, unlike that which I have been hearing from the other side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), in his address to which I listened with great interest, referred to the Avro Arrow and the dismantling of that project. That matter was picked up by another member of his Party. I would like to ask the Leader of the New Democratic Party what he thinks of that project within the current framework of peace negotiations and the world concern for peace.
1 understand that the Avro Arrow was a weapon of war. That is to say, it was to be used in the National Defence program and had the capacity to carry bombs of great destructive capacity. Apart from the technology involved, and I understand the Hon. member's interest in that, is he interested in arming Canada more and involving it in the international defence industry? Does he want Canadians to participate in weapons of war and to build up and industry of national destruction, or does he want us to pursue peacefully industrial interests that employ people and keep Canadians in industries that will guarantee employment over this decade and future decades? Does he want us to engage again in the international arms race with weapons with a capacity for total destruction?

Mr. Speaker, Conservative Members certainly are the masters of the irrelevant question. I would say to the Hon. Member quite clearly that we happen to differ in
certain details of defence policy. That is the difference between a Government Party and an opposition Party. The New Democratic Party believes in a defence policy. We believe that, regrettably so, in a modern world we still need weapons. However, unlike certain other parts of the world-I will not make a polemical point about the Government. Not only do we believe in the defence of Canada, we also believe that we ought to be working simultaneously for disarmament in the world. Those two things are not mutually exclusive.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a question with the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) regarding his position that the national Government should own Crown corporations. In the Province of Manitoba, the Minister responsible for Crown corporations went to The Netherlands last month in order to try to sell a Crown corporation called Llyer Industries. He made the statement before the Economic Committee of the Legislature that he would sell Llyer Industries and that if he could not sell it he would close it down. Who was with the Minister in The Netherlands but a union leader from Llyer Industries.
Has the Leader of the NDP been writing to Mr. Pawley to tell him not to close down Llyer Industries? Has the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) been writing to Mr. Pawley to tell him not to close down Llyer Industries? If they are not doing that, how can they rise in the House to make statements like the one the Hon. Member just made?

Mr. Speaker, I would make a couple of points in reply to the Hon. Member. I note that he said that a union member was being consulted and was part of what was going on. That is in complete and utter contrast to what the Conservative Government has done in this case. The Government did not have the thoughtfulness to consult the workers at all. If the Government of Manitoba is doing that, it is to be commended.
I hope the Hon. Member listened to my argument. I was not arguing that Crown corporations should never be sold back to the private sector. I never said such a thing. In fact, I gave as one of the options at which we should look the desirability of selling the firm to the private sector and making sure the taxpayers got a good deal, but I made the point that it should be sold to the Canadian private sector and remain Canadian owned.
Third, in my judgment-and I am not an expert but I have seen the experiences elsewhere in the world-regarding whether certain sectors ought to be privately or publicly owned, world experience seems to suggest that public ownership in this sector which massively involves taxpayers' money probably makes sense. It is a question of detail. We are unequivocally clear that this industry ought to remain Canadian owned. We think that on balance it ought to remain in the public sector but we have not closed the door to having it sold to a Canadian firm. If the Manitoba Government in its wisdom-I'm not there, I'm not from that province and I do not know the details-happens to believe that that particular Crown corpo-
December 3, 1985

ration would be more viable and effective for the people of Manitoba in the private sector, that could well be the perfectly sensible solution.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Government announced that the de Havilland Corporation, which is located in Downsview which is in my riding, was to be sold to the Boeing Corporation and that a 90-day long memorandum of intent had been signed for that purpose. I would like to indicate, as have commentators all across the country overnight, that this is a tragedy of the order of the one committed by a former Conservative Government which closed down the production of the Avro Arrow, putting something like 15,000 people out of work. This is not a decision that will put 15,000 people out of work as did the Avro-Arrow decision, and I will speak of that in a moment. I will not criticize Boeing although I will say something about it. However, I would like to assure the House and Canadian people that this is no less a tragedy, the consequences being the diminution of the economy of the country, the reduction of Canadian sovereignty and the subtraction from the Canadian identity, which are as serious as those of the tragic closing down of the Avro Arrow.
The de Havilland Corporation is a company located in my riding which uses suppliers from virtually every province in the country. All Canadians are a part of it and apart from their physical, technological and working contributions, it is a part of the Canadian identity. This is the company which made the Twin Otter and the Beaver. This is the company which made the Mosquito. These are a line of planes which particularly define the Canadian way of approaching aerospace, something which the company has been doing over the decades. The idea that this company will become a division of a multinational firm, however good that firm is, has closed the door on the future for all Canadians.
I said that I wished to talk about Boeing for a moment. Boeing is a good company. It is a good multinational corporation. Boeing manufactures the most successful passenger and cargo jet airplanes in the world. It has sold more of certain of its lines, more copies of some of its planes, than other planes which have been produced in the world. This is to Boeing's credit, and I do not want to criticize the company. However, in this connection I wish to point out that it seems to have adapted well to doing business in Canada. One of its first acts following the election of the Conservative Government was to engage as its public relations firm the firm of Advance Planning. Advance Planning is a subsidiary of Camp and Associates which was set up at the time of the Government's coming to power. Camp and Associates is a Canadian company whose identity with the Conservative Party is well known. If anything, one could give credit to Boeing for understanding how the new Government operates. Boeing put itself in the ballpark through the use of a public relations firm which is known and friendly to the Government.
1 also wish to point out that it must be helpful for Boeing to establish a base in Canada which is larger than the base it had
Supply
in the past. After all, with the whole future of jobs at de Havilland at stake, from now on if this deal goes through- and I hope it will not-Boeing will be in a position months and years from now to remind the Government that it is the owner of this large enterprise in Toronto. Boeing will be able to remind the Government that de Havilland is a division of its company and that if Air Canada is looking for other types of airplanes made by other companies, or if the Department of National Defence is in the same position, then Boeing may also remind the Government that it is the company keeping jobs at de Havilland in Toronto. That is the regrettable fact of this acquisition by Boeing. Again, I make no criticism of Boeing because of that possibility. However, it does show that the Government has given Boeing a hostage for future performances which will be favourable to it.
1 indicated that this acquisition is a tragedy of a diffrent order when compared to the loss of 15,000 jobs. Ironically, I am positive that at least in the foreseeable future there will be big increases in terms of employment at the Downsview air base. When I was there yesterday for the announcement by management I learned that 34 new employees were taken on just yesterday. I learned that 50 employees were taken on that day. I learned that 1,000 have been taken on over the last year. The reason for this is not the sale which was announced yesterday. The reason is that de Havilland has finally reached the stage where its Dash-8 is ready to take off.
The taxpayers of Canada brought this company through the worst recession since the 1930s, that is, from 1981 until today. It was brought through that recession with a good workforce, with all its research capacity intact, with all its management in place and with products for which orders are finally starting to roll in large numbers. In order to justify the development costs there needs to be 400 sales of the Dash-8. As a result of the planes and as a result of the confidence which Canadians had in the company over the years, and not as a result of anything the Government or Boeing has done, de Havilland is now in a position where it has nearly 200 sales. I also learned yesterday that the Twin Otter, which has been out of production for a few years, is being brought back into production in a new modernized version adapted to today's requirements. 1 also learned yesterday that the production of the Dash-7 will be speeded up as well. I learned that the Dash-7 Stretch is now considered to be more viable, and while it is still on the drawing boards it has been given a great boost.
So there will be jobs created over the next few months. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) cannot get up, nor can the Government, in the months ahead and say these results are because of the takeover. It is because of the products. It is because of the confidence which Canadians have had in the company over the last few years.
The company will now be owned by an American corporation if the deal goes through. 1 have already indicated that Boeing is a good company. Hawker Siddeley was a good company too. It owned de Havilland until 1974. I would like to remind the Government of the reason the company was taken over by the former Liberal Government from Hawker Sidde-

ley. It was not taken over because the former Government was fanatically committed to state ownership. It was taken over because the Hawker Siddeley multinational corporation had more important priorities than the products which were being created at de Havilland in Downsview. Hawker Siddeley had other planes which it was making in the United Kingdom, just as Boeing has other planes it is making in the United States. At a certain point in time Hawker Siddeledy decided it was not prepared to take its shareholders' investment and capital and invest it in Canada in the research which had been done in terms of the continuation of the STOL lines. That is not an improper decision for a multinational corporation to take. I think it was wrong. Hawker Siddeley should have stuck with the STOL aircraft which de Havilland had designed and begun to produce. However, when it did not do so, the former Government moved in and took the company over.
Now that we are realizing the privatization dream of the new Conservative Government, and since this company will become a division of the Boeing Aircraft Corporation, how can it be denied that the greater priorities of the multinational corporation will not prevail? How can this be done when, in Seattle, where Boeing sells its planes, it sells one which costs more than the whole purchase price of de Havilland Aircraft? When capital is short and when de Havilland needed good managers and wanted good research people, which they find here in Canada, please do not kid us, Government, and tell us that Boeing will not come to Canada and draw on the strengths of de Havilland for its multinational purposes. That would be the normal thing for a multinational corporation to do and we will suffer for it.
I remind the Government that de Havilland accounts for 25 per cent of the aerospace industry in Canada. The act which was announced yesterday-yesterday's tragedy-takes the company out of the control of Canadians and puts it into the control of a company with large scale priorities when, someday soon, like Hawker Siddeley, it just might decide that de Havilland is less important to it than its other affairs in the United States.
What have we lost? The autonomy of the company has been diminished. It was its autonomy which permitted the design of these airplanes in the first place. Canadian identity is lessened since we are proud of these planes, as we have a right to be. The taxpayers of Canada have paid large sums of money to keep this company going and to keep its products going. It is no longer part of the Canadian identity. Canadian sovereignty is reduced as a result of the sale announced yesterday by the Government. That is the tragedy.
When he spoke the Leader of the New Democratic Party reminded us that he comes from Oshawa. I was thinking about that while he was speaking. Back in the 1920s, the McLaughlin Automobile Company, the last major Canadian automotive company, was sold to a multinational firm. But jobs did not go down, jobs went up. There are more people working in Canada in the automotive industry now than were working in that industry when McLaughlin owned that company. When I said that our sovereignty and identity were diminished, what I was
getting at was that when that last company was sold-not by the Government but by the owners-Canadians lost the opportunity to express themselves through the economy, the opportunity to create products which would have responded to our situation and not to the situation of our powerful neighbours to the south.
Would the Canadian automobile have been a Volkswagon, a Rolls-Royce, a Volvo? I do not know the answers to that question. And, starting today, we will never know what Canada might have contributed to the world in aerospace. We made a pretty good start; the Twin-Otter, the Dash 7 and the Dash 8. These are pretty good expressions of Canada's way of dealing with aerospace in the world today. But we will not know from now on how Canadian identity would have developed in this sector because this Government does not see the difference between a Canadian owner and a foreign owner.
I agree with a lot of things the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) said today, but David Lewis once said in this House, before his Party became excited about economic sovereignty: "There is no differnece between a Canadian capitalist and an American capitalist. They both want to be as efficient as possible and to make as much money as possible". My Party has never left it at that. We think there is a difference between Canadian ownership and foreign ownership.
While we feel that this is not the moment to sell, we do feel that if it is going to privatize-and 1 am going to come to the Canadian option in a moment-why not find a Canadian solution? Why not keep an election promise? During the last election campaign the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)-and he is not here in the House today-promised on behalf of his Party that there would be a national aerospace company. He promised that de Havilland and Canadair would be put together, that they would be made viable by converting liabilities to paid in or contributed surplus, and so on, and shares would be offered to the Canadian people. That promise looked pretty good for the Canadian people, but we have heard nothing about it. What has happened? Why is it not still a good idea to take the company and put it together with Canadair, make a Canadian company and allow the Canadian people to express their confidence in the aerospace industry by taking a risk as investors in the future of a corporation like that?
Why is the Government not doing that? There is no explanation. The Government has made the announcement, after secret negotiations into which it would not even bring the management of the company 100 per cent, nor would it bring in the United Auto Workers, not to mention an interested Canadian bidder. In secret the Government has made a deal and has produced a memorandum of agreement which it has not shown us and which I am asking today that it make public so that during this 90 day period-if it is such a good deal- we can have a look at it.
I would like to say a few words about the price, and my colleagues will speak about that as well. It is obvious that the
December 3, 1985

price puts no value at all on the product lines and on all of the development costs which the company wrote off, thanks to the taxpayers of Canada. These are being handed over to the Boeing Corporation for free. But even if the price were much higher, I cannot see the justification for this sale because the Canadian Government is going to continue to stand behind these aircraft and this company. From what we have heard the Government say, it will continue to support it like it supports every other high-tech company in Canada, and it is going to do more than the Export Development Corporation usually does to help foreign sales. Boeing, apparently, has been able to negotiate that. The Government is going to continue to insure all of the aircraft which have been produced by the company. That is a very big ticket cost. Therefore, Boeing is taking money out of one pocket and handing it to the Canadian Government-not enough as far as I am concerned-but even if it were more, the Canadian Government is still taking a lot of our money and putting it into the other pocket of Boeing to encourage that company to buy us out, to take over de Havilland.
I would like to tell the Government that it has to come up with something beyond financial consideration and beyond taking a load off its agenda in order to justify this sale.
What 1 think, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government is desperate to validate the promise it made that it would privatize companies. It has looked around and has not been able to sell anything. It is desperate and it has sold this company. I want to ask why the Government has not given the Rimgate group, a Canadian-based group, all of the information Boeing was given so that that group could make a sensible offer for the company? 1 have spoken to the Rimgate group. It has given me chapter and verse on the things it has not been told which have been told to the Boeing group.

Unlike Boeing, the Rimgate Group was not given details of the performance of this company. No promises were made regarding further investments to be made by the Government. I would like to ask the Government, during this 90-day period, to give Rimgate the same information and the same opportunity to make an offer as Boeing was given.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on behalf of the Government in the debate today, and I have no hesitation in stating that the motion presented by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) is unfounded and entirely without substance.
Contrary to what the motion says, instead of abandoning the aerospace industry in this country, the Government, in taking the step announced yesterday, has expressed its confidence in the future of an industry that is very important to this country. By proposing the sale of de Havilland Aircraft Ltd. to Boeing, an internationally known company, a company that is financially and managerially sound, a company that has a thorough knowledge of the industry throughout the world, by agreeing to this merger, the Government is providing Canadian industry with a far greater potential for participation in international markets.
This Government fully recognizes the importance of the aerospace industry to Canada. Judging by the wording of the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) I wonder whether he has any real understanding or recognition of the true significance of that industry.
In his motion he seems to characterize the aerospace industry as consisting solely of de Havilland. While de Havilland is very obviously an important company and will be even more important in the future as a result of the Government's creative move announced yesterday, we should not lose sight of the fact that 45,000 Canadians are employed in the aerospace industry that is made up of more than 100 companies from coast to coast.
We are proud of the performance of workers, of engineers and of the management of de Havilland who have built for that company a world-wide reputation in the manufacture of commuter aircraft. For the Leader of the New Democratic Party to ignore and neglect the contribution of other elements of the industry, an oversight of which he is clearly guilty when one looks at his motion accusing the Government of "abandoning the aerospace industry", I wonder if he would like to go with me to visit these other fine companies and tell them and their workers that in his eyes they just do not rate as vital components of the Canadian aerospace industry.
Let him tell that to the workers of Canadair in Montreal, the workers of Boeing in Winnipeg and Arnprior, the workers of Pratt and Whitney, the workers of McDonnell-Douglas, the workers of CAE, Spar Aerospace and Fleet Aerospace or the relative newcomers to Canada like British Aerospace or the many other companies that contribute to the human and financial resources and the advancement of this industry.
December 3, 1985



Mr. Speaker, the fact is that this Government is well aware of its commitment to all sectors of the Canadian aerospace industry. We are not only respecting these commitments, we are doing more than that by ensuring greater viability for an industry that is so important to the high technology sector in Canada.

The Leader of the New Democratic Party makes two unfounded and unsupported allegations in his motion. Allow me to deal with both of them and I will refute them totally and completely. First, he accuses us of abandoning the Canadian aerospace industry through the privatization of de Havilland and the sale to Boeing. Second, he accuses us of failing to protect aerospace technology paid for by the Canadian taxpayers and developed by de Havilland.
I have already shown that the Hon. Member has no grasp or understanding of the breadth of the Canadian aerospace industry. Now I will show that far from abandoning the Canadian aerospace industry we have taken the only sensible and realistic course; to bring to an end at de Havilland a decade of increasing financial losses paid for by the taxpayers. These losses, if allowed to continue, could lead only to the ultimate and final wind-up of the company and the loss of the existing jobs.
It should be evident, even to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, that de Havilland was at a critical point. Despite strong products and the dedication of its employees, new product development and new investment and even a new direction were urgently required.
de Havilland's traditional private line, which stood the company in good stead in the past, needed updating. Sales of the Dash-7 peaked at 107, with only a handful of additional orders on the books. While the company had received approximately 117 orders and options for the Dash-8, only 13 had been delivered to date.
de Havilland's losses for the first nine months of this year stood at $55 million on top of losses of $76 million last year before a special tax credit. To date, the federal Government committed more than $834 million of public funds to the company. If we were to continue to keep the company in the public sector, further substantial tax moneys would be required, to our best estimate probably some $200 million for next year alone in new capital investment and to cover ongoing operating losses.
The Government faced these choices: continuing to allow the company to absorb hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars every year; closing it down completely at a further cost of hundreds of millions of dollars, not to mention the loss of jobs and the terrible social and economic impact that such a closure would have; or finding a buyer in the private sector with the financial clout, the commitment, the ability, the energy and know how to ensure that de Havilland would remain a company that would prosper and have an open door to the market of commuter airlines throughout the world.

[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, 1 can assure you that the Government is entirely aware of the significant investment of taxpayers' money in de Havilland. And to protect that investment in Canada's aerospace technology, the Government has negotiated with Boeing a world product mandate for de Havilland, including not only the Dash-7 and the Dash-8 but all products that may derive therefrom.

Anyone who was at the news conference yesterday heard Mr. Albrecht, Chairman of the Board of Boeing Canada, publicly commit his company to proceed with a Stretch version of the Dash-8. That is an investment that will no doubt involve sums in the magnitude of several hundred million dollars. It will mean more jobs at de Havilland and more jobs at the hundreds of suppliers across Canada who serve de Havilland. That is how we are protecting the Canadian aerospace industry. That is how we are protecting Canadian technology. That is how we are protecting existing jobs and making sure that we will be creating more jobs in this industry as we have done throughout the country in the last 15 months.
We have made it clear through the privatization process to which the Government is committed that privatization will strengthen the ability of our commercially oriented Crown corporations to compete in the market-place.
We on this side of the House recognize the reality of the market-place. We recognize that by reducing the bureaucratic and political impediments, there will be a more effective allocation of resources in a more efficient market economy. Above all, we recognize that through privatization we can enassure that the maximum benefits flow to Canadians in terms of jobs and new investment while reducing as far as possible the risks and exposure that taxpayers may face in supporting some of these industries.
In the case of de Havilland, I have reported that the Government contacted more than 130 prospective buyers. After a year of intensive efforts, three offers to purchase were received and studied carefully. In selecting Boeing, I would like to stress that not only did we select the company that made the best offer, we also selected a company with an outstanding and proven track record as a good corporate citizen of Canada. Boeing's relationship with this country goes back some 66 years. Throughout that period of time, Boeing has always behaved itself as we would expect any upstanding true Canadian corporation to behave.
The letter of intent setting out the basis for the sale of de Havilland to Boeing has many important features. It includes undertakings that will keep de Havilland in Ontario, that will require Boeing to pay royalties to Canada on existing products and assign to de Havilland a world product mandate, to develop new activities at de Havilland and work with Canadian suppliers across the country. All these features are designed to ensure the further development of the Canadian aerospace industry, not its abandonment.
9062

December 3, 1985
Supply
This initiative both secures the future of de Havilland and marks a major step for the Canadian aerospace industry, a $4 billion industry which is already the fifth largest in the industrial world.
In brief, we have reached a successful conclusion to our year-long quest to re-establish de Havilland in the private sector under ownership which has an impeccable record in the aerospace industry. The Boeing Company, by its financial and marketing commitment to de Havilland, demonstrates more faith in the future of Canada than does the mover of this motion. If the purchase of de Havilland turns out to be a good deal for Boeing shareholders-and I sincerely trust that it will-it will also turn out to be a good deal for Canada, de Havilland will be a good deal for its shareholders only when it is profitable. That will be a good deal for the taxpayers of Canada because for the first time they will begin to receive reimbursement through the taxes which a profitable de Havilland will be paying for all the support given it over the past decade.
Far from abandoning the aerospace industry, the Government is strengthening that vital industry. Far from failing to protect Canadian aerospace technology, the Government is ensuring that de Havilland technology will enjoy a wider window on the markets of the world.
The privatization of de Havilland sends a strong message that the Government is determined to remove the shadows which have bound significant portions of Canada's industrial economy. Through our privatization program, we will be able to allow organizations, which were once restricted to government control, to build their own futures in ways that will benefit both their employees and the investors who demonstrate, by their financial commitment, their confidence in the future of our great country.
In conclusion, let me repeat that the motion put forward by the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party and amended by the Hon. Member of the Liberal Party is without foundation. It is hardly deserving of the attention of the House. I know that it will be relegated to the obscurity it so richly deserves.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board about the commitment made during the election campaign by the present Minister of Finance that the de Havilland Corporation and Canadair would be put together into a national aerospace company, and that shares of that company would be offered for subscription directly to Canadian people. Why did the Government turn its back on that commitment? If it did not, what effort did it make before abandoning it to try to deliver on that promise?

Mr. Speaker, in terms of the process of privatization, in the first step, the line Ministers responsible for various Crown corporations evaluate each of their respective Crown corporations to see whether or not they fit the definition which we use for candidacy for privatization, in other words, is the company commercial, and does the company effectively no longer fulfil a public policy purpose? The company is also evaluated from a financial point of view. It is proposed to the task force and, if it is accepted, the second stage of the process is an in-depth evaluation of the prospects of that company and the resolution of financial and policy issues which can arise during the privatization process. Only after that first stage is the company really put up for sale, bids are entertained, analyses of the bids are made and finally the commitment for sale is made.
We followed this process in this case, as we did in the other cases which we have announced to date. It was felt that in terms of ensuring a vigorous and vibrant aerospace industry in the country, the best way to go was the sale of de Havilland to the Boeing Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, in other words, no consideration at all was given by the Government to the promise made during the election campaign. I heard from the Hon. Minister that they gave no attention at all to that promise. They started from scratch, just as if no promise had been made.
The Minister indicated a bright future for de Havilland. I hope he is right. Has the Government done any calculation in that bright future of the production and development of Stretch Dash-8? If things go as well as he suggested they might for the company, how much money will the Canadian Government put into it, in all the various ways the Government supports industrial activity in the country?

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the company will be eligible for the various programs for which all other companies in that industry, or for that matter in other industries, are eligible. I am sure that in the development of the company we will be looking at requests under existing programs for government assistance of the same nature, on the same footing and of the same conditions as any other Canadian corporate entity could request.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister. He referred to the fact that he anticipated de Havilland would be paying taxes. Could he name a single major producer of aircraft anywhere in the world, in terms of net, which is paying taxes to its Government? In that context, was he aware that the Boeing Corporation, in the last two years for which data was available, in spite of a book profit of $1.5 billion, did not pay a cent in income tax because of the tax structure for this kind of industry in the United States, and in fact received in that period of time $400 million in assistance from the American Government in tax policy? Is he aware of those facts?

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware of the balance sheet and of the profit and loss statement of the Boeing Corporation. Obviously, when one concludes as important a transaction as this one, it is only prudent management for the seller to ensure that the purchaser is enjoying fine
December 3, 1985

financial health. 1 can only reassure the Hon. Member that such is the case; Boeing is in fact a financially very strong and healthy corporation. I would like to be able to say the same for de Havilland. At the moment it is not. We firmly believe that with this deal,with this transaction and with the existing financial strength of Boeing, we will see within a short period of time a company in Canada, in Ontario, in Downsview, which will also have an interesting profit and loss statement.
There is no question. Boeing would not buy this corporation if it thought it would lose money forever. It intends to make money with that company. It intends to make profits. When it makes profits, it will pay taxes under our tax structure.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister clearly missed the point or chose not to deal with it. The point I was making was that because of the tax structures of different countries, including the United States of America, these corporations end up not paying taxes at all in that they are subsidized one way or another by taxpayers. All the Minister has done is use Canadian taxpayers' money to put over $800 million, according to the updated figures which the Minister gave the House today, into this company. That has already gone from Canadian taxpayers. What Boeing is getting is a gift of a couple of aircraft, and we paid for the development of them. Boeing will build on that. Given the structure which the Government is about to set up for the corporation, it will make lots of profit in Canada because all the costs have already been written off by Canadian taxpayers.
I have another question for the Minister. I know he is ultimately interested in-and I do not say it facetiously-a factual presentation; we can have a dispute about the policy. However, earlier he alluded to my equating the aerospace industry in Canada with the existing facilities at de Havilland. Would he acknowledge that in my speech and in reply to questions therafter, even before he spoke, I talked about the more than 100 firms in this industry in Canada and also the fact that there were some 40,000 people already employed; in short, that I did not ignore other companies in this sector?

Mr. Speaker, I will acknowledge that in his questions the Hon. Member did allude to the fact that there are some 40,000 people employed in the aerospace industry in the country. I am happy that he acknowledged that. It is an important industry which we would like to have grow and prosper in the country. We feel that the move we announced yesterday is a move in that direction which will ensure that, rather than declining, the number of employees will grow over the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask about the Fokker company in particular, a Dutch manufacturer. The Minister said that 130 companies were canvassed to see if they would be interested in taking de Havilland off the Government's hands. One of the companies was Fokker. Yet, when Fokker appeared again as part of a Canadian bidding group, I understand that the CD1C refused to give details to the group because Fokker

was part of it, although it would have been prepared to give Fokker information directly. Does the Minister understand, as I do, that the Canadian bidding group was not given full information because of something to do with the presence of Fokker, which makes a somewhat similar airplane, and yet the Government was prepared to tell all to de Havilland when it was one of the 130 companies with no Canadian involvement at all?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make something very clear. From the phrasing of the Hon. Member's question, it is obvious that there is a misunderstanding in his mind. In this transaction, as in any transaction to come, we would never divulge to a direct competitor information that deals directly with the product against which he is competing.
Why did you approach Fokker in the first place?

We would not have given that part of the information to Fokker.
With regard to the second question, the group in which Fokker was involved got all the co-operation it could possibly request from the CDIC. The only exception was some specific product information which could have been used in a competitive environment to the detriment of de Havilland. I repeat that that kind of information would not be made available to a prospective buyer of any of the Crown corporations which we contemplate selling over the months and years to come.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) mentioned that Advance Planning, part of Camp and Associates in Toronto, was the public relations firm for Boeing. Could the Minister outline what part they played in the negotiations and whether they were paid on a commission basis? It seems that Boeing has paid an incredibly low price. If the Minister feels that he has, as he indicated today, made such a great sale, would he be willing to put the issue before Parliament within 90 days for the approval of the House?

Mr. Speaker, in response to the first question, I am not aware of the specifics of the relationship the Hon. Member alluded to. I will be happy to try to get the information for him, but I do not have it with me.

speechtext: The period for questions and comments is now terminated. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) on debate.

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the comments of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) who said that the motion of the

December 3, 1985
Supply
New Democratic Party was without substance. 1 was interested in that because in the debate which took place in the Ontario Legislature yesterday the Minister's political comrade, Larry Grossman, the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario, said quite specifically that David Peterson had not done enough to keep the plant in Canadian hands. He quite clearly took the view that Ontario should have been doing more and I presume that he meant that his federal colleagues should have been doing more as well. Perhaps there is a division on the Conservative side, but it seems to me that Mr. Grossman feels that the concerns reflected in my Party-about this deal have some substance.
I note as well that when the Dash-8 was first rolled out, Bill Davis, then the Premier of Ontario, said that de Havilland must continue to be part of the economic life of this great country. I am sure that he meant it should remain in Canadian hands. In fact, that is quite specifically what his successor, Frank Miller, promised. During his term as leader he suggested that Ontario should buy de Havilland if that was necessary to prevent de Havilland from leaving Canada or being sold out from Canadian ownership.
I would like to talk about the issues raised by this sell-out at bargain basement prices. It echoes the Conservative's destruction of the Avro Arrow 25 years ago. I believe that many years from now people will look back on this week as a dark, dark week in the history of Canada because one of the leading companies in the Canadian aerospace industry went out of Canadian hands. Of course, there are 100 or more part suppliers in the industry but they will not be able to continue to work effectively if we take away the few companies which are in fact assembling final products or assembling and designing aircraft. De Havilland was the only Canadian company which was able to conceive, design, implement, and bring to market a completely Canadian-designed aircraft. The Dash-7, the Dash-8, and the others which have been mentioned are fine examples.
Canadair has been responsible for production of the CF-18 but that is a plane designed in the United States for which the components are largely made in the United States as well. Canadair has the Challenger jet on the market, but that, too, is a product of U.S. technology and U.S. know how which was brought in by Canadair. de Havilland is our only distinctively Canadian company with distinctive competence in the aircraft industry, and now it is being sold to Boeing.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Government's defence of this particular deal is weak and that a lot of questions have been raised. If the Government were to come clean and provide us with all the information, we might be able, even now, to point to other directions which could have been taken rather than selling de Havilland to Boeing at bargain sale prices.
I will put this into terms which people may be able to understand a bit better. The price of a Dash-8 is about $6 million American or about $8 million Canadian. Boeing is buying the de Havilland Corporation for $90 million Canadian, which is equivalent to the price of about 11 Dash-8s or
about six months production. That is how cheaply Boeing is getting de Havilland. It is quite clear that the $65 million deferred note to which Boeing is committing itself can and will be worked out by means of a modest 16 per cent increase in its current volume of purchases in Canada, according to the information that we have been given. Therefore, Boeing gets the company for next to nothing.
What else does Boeing get? The President of the Treasury Board did not talk about the other ways in which the Canadian taxpayer will continue to be committed to subsidizing de Havilland while it is in American hands. We are giving Boeing a $400 million or $500 million tax write-off due to tax losses of de Havilland over the course of the last three or four years. Those tax losses are like money in the bank, Mr. Speaker. They guarantee that, if de Havilland has profits, it will not have to pay a nickel in Canadian tax for the next 15 or 20 years. Although I am not quite clear on this because the details have not been given to us, those tax write-offs may well be transferred by Boeing to its other Canadian operations. It is clear, however, that those tax write-offs will have the effect of saving Boeing between $150 million and $200 million in taxes over the course of the next decade or two. That means that for $90 million Boeing gets tax write-offs worth $150 million or $200 million.
On top of that Boeing will get a $30 million commitment from the Government of Canada to cover product liabilities on the existing fleet of aircraft which has already been built and sent to market. If this deal had been done in a businesslike way, Boeing would have taken over the liabilities of the corporation it acquired. In this case, the Government of Canada is taking back some of those obligations to the tune of $30 million.
When I look at the finances involved in this deal, it is hard to believe how little we are receiving for the $700 million or $800 million we poured into de Havilland over the course of the last 12 years since the company was acquired from its British parent. We have poured that money in and Boeing has now picked up not one but two aircraft which are completely developed. It has also picked up the Buffalo and the Twin Otter, aircraft for which markets continue to exist from time to time. The development costs of these aircraft have been completely paid for.
Today I spoke to someone from Wall Street and 1 asked an expert in the aerospace industry to ask him to evaluate the deal. He pointed out that it was obvious that the output of de Havilland complemented the product line of Boeing. However, in all of the time Boeing has been making aircraft since the first commercial jets were rolled off the assembly line by Bell-Boeing back around 1959 it has stayed away from the field of building commuter aircraft and short take-off and landing aircraft, the aircraft in which de Havilland has chosen to specialize. That is why I find a number of the things in the promises and commitments made and the rationale put for-
December 3, 1985

ward by the Government for this particular deal to be pretty hollow.
It has been said that de Havilland will have a world product mandate for producing commuter aircraft. It has that already. Boeing is not competing in that particular area. If in 25 years Boeing has not gone into that area, it was because it had other interests. It may well cost half a billion dollars to begin building commuter aircraft. That is why Boeing had not chosen to go into that particular sector of the market. Now it is getting into that sector of the market for free or just about for free. It is no wonder it snapped up the opportunity to buy de Havilland when it was offered for sale by the Government of Canada.
The President of the Treasury Board suggested that de Havilland would be able to benefit from the world-wide marketing of the Boeing Corporation. However, de Havilland was already marketing its aircraft around the world. In the course of the last nine months, of the 27 aircraft that rolled out of de Havilland's facilities in Downsview, all but three were sold to the export market. In fact, de Havilland was in the process of establishing an aerospace facility in Singapore because of its growing market in Southeast Asia. It was already marketing around the world and was not being barred or blocked from marketing around the world because of the fact that it was a Canadian company. There were no restraints. There could be restraints now that de Havilland will be under the control of the Boeing Corporation. We already know how many Canadian companies are restrained from selling into their most logical natural markets in the United States because of prohibitions laid upon them by their parent corporations.
In his defence of this deal, the President of the Treasury Board has suggested that there were only two options. In other words, the Government blinkered itself in the end into saying that only two things could be done: one was to shut down de Havilland and the other was to sell it. The Leader of my Party has already spoken of other options. There could have been joint ventures with the private sector or sharing agreements with Boeing. If Boeing did not have a line of commuter aircraft it could sell and if it wanted to look for economies of scale in terms of marketing, servicing and sales support, there would have been a logical connection between the two companies. That should and could have been discussed. However, the Government did not want to see it that particular way.
Canadian purchasers were specifically ruled out of this sale because of the Government's requirement that any bidder had to have airframe manufacturing expertise and financial depth. It was not mentioned publicly, but any bidder also had to have another line of profitable business against which it could offset the tax losses which were ready to be tapped in the de Havilland package.
When Canadair was refinanced a year or so ago, the former Government set it up as old Canadair and new Canadair. New Canadair is profitable because of the fact that its capital obligations to the Government were taken over and it is a separate entity under the wing of the Canada Development Investment Corporation. If that had been done in the case of
Supply
de Havilland, then I would suggest that the price to be paid for it might have been different. It might even have been more attractive to Canadian buyers who would not stand to benefit from the tax losses but who, on the other hand, would prefer to put their investment in de Havilland into development of a new product line and the improvement of its equipment in ways that have been discussed by various Members of the House. That option was clearly not put forward.
The Government said that a purchaser had to take the whole thing lock, stock and barrel, and the carrot was that in addition to getting fully developed aircraft, a buyer of the scale and scope of McDonnell Douglas or Boeing would also be able to get all those juicy, fat tax losses. The businessmen on the board of the Canada Development Investment Corporation who, we are told, endorsed this particular bid, would look at it as if it were a purely private-sector operation.
My Party says quite explicitly that this is not a purely private-sector operation. We are talking about the future of the aerospace industry in Canada. We are talking about whether or not the present Government has any idea of what kind of industry it wishes to see developed over the course of the coming years. This is the vision that is lacking by the present Government. It confined its judgment on this decision to a group of private-sector directors who happened to be drawing their fees by working for the CDIC. Then the former president of a bank, who is now the President of the Treasury Board, decided that that was a good thing, recommended the deal to Cabinet, Cabinet endorsed it, and now the deal is going to go forward apparently without intervention from Investment Canada.
If de Havilland was a subsidiary of a Canadian company, if it was experiencing losses and difficulties in the aerospace market, a market which is not an easy one, and if it was experiencing problems because of competition from subsidized aviation companies from other countries, then a decision to sell out to Boeing, Douglas, Fokker, or some other purchaser might have been entirely justified. I would suggest that a company that is a key company in the aerospace sector because of its buying power and the impact of its research and development throughout the aerospace sector of Canada cannot be dealt with by the Government on that basis.
My research into and thinking this particular area have told me that there are a number of key national industries including automobile, electronics and aerospace industries which are increasingly competing world-wide one with the other in a way that individual corporations used to compete against each other a few years ago. If Canada does not understand that the industrial strategy for a particular industry must be designed and implemented on a national basis, then we are going to find ourselves unable to compete with other countries that see things that way and practise industrial strategies in that manner. It is no secret that the Government of Japan, through the Ministry of International Trade and Industry, does exactly that. It has helped industries to grow and has cut back on industries by looking at them not on a company-by-company

December 3, 1985
Supply
basis but at how the industry as a whole is competing against the same industries of other nations. We are not doing that.
According to the judgment expressed in this deal to sell de Havilland to Boeing, we are simply saying that it is possible for Canada to continue to exist in the 1960s while the rest of the world moves on to the 1990s. There are grave risks inherent in that particular approach.
A bit later, my colleagues will speak about some of our specific concerns with this deal. We are concerned over the fact that vague promises were made but there are no job guarantees for the 4,150 workers of de Havilland. When Rimgate Holdings of Vancouver, a Canadian company that bid on this particular deal, made its offer, it indicated that it was prepared to guarantee a minimum of 3,500 jobs at de Havilland. No such guarantees have come from Boeing in this particular case.
We are concerned with the fact that the public could-and we think should-have either retained ownership or else retained a share in de Havilland in order to ensure that it continued to serve Canadian interests in terms of the development of technology, continued to retain Canadian jobs and in terms of ensuring that sourcing was done here in Canada.
1 do not agree with my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), who suggests that a Canadian capitalist is no different from an American capitalist. I often find they are almost the same. However, if we had a choice I would prefer ownership to remain here in Canada where, as a Government, we can have some influence upon the company. One matter 1 find particularly objectionable with respect to this deal is the fact that, once the sale is consummated, Canada's potential for influencing or controlling what happens in this key area of this important industry will effectively be zero.
There are no enforceable guarantees which we can see in the deal. All of the information which has been given to us suggests that some vague and glowing promises may have been made by Boeing; but there is no way that these promises will be implemented if Boeing decides to back away from the deal.
It was somewhat ironic to hear the industry critic for the Liberal Party talk yesterday about how Boeing had established a firm with regional development grants in Winnipeg in order to be at the leading edge of fibreglass technology for the aerospace industry. The former Minister said: "Is it not terrible that all it is doing is making fibreglass bathtubs?" That was something which came about under the Liberal Government. It found it was not able or prepared to enforce any type of agreements with Boeing. At least at that time there was some effort to put the agreement down in writing. In this case it is just an agreement to sell and very little will be left in order to enforce the deal.
I say to the taxpayers of Canada with respect to this particular deal: "Hang on to your wallets". With respect to the deal, the Government makes the argument that it is a good deal and, anyway, it is spending a great deal on de Havilland,
much more than it thought the taxpayers should be required to spend. It is interesting that a different argument was made when the Reichmann family spoke about the Canadianization of Gulf Canada and through Olympia & York was given a tax deal which will cost the taxpayers $600 million-all this to increase Canadian ownership in the oil industry and to allow the Reichmanns to take control of Gulf Canada. I am not sure why this different standard applies but it is interesting to note that, in fact, Boeing is a champion free-loader when it comes to taking advantage of government funds in the United States. I suspect we may find that it is just as eager to take advantage of government programs here in Canada.
In the period from 1981 to 1984 Boeing made profits in excess of $2 billion. Of 50 highly profitable corporations it was the champion in terms of generating income tax refunds from the federal Government. It did not pay a nickel in tax, yet it received $285 million in tax refunds from the U.S. federal Government between 1981 and 1984. That does not speak to the fact that the Americans have an industrial strategy, in terms of encouraging the development of large private corporations such as Boeing. This is not done through the process of industrial grants and regional expansion grants. We are criticized by the Americans for carrying out that type of action in terms of implementing a social strategy in Canada. Boeing benefits from defence industry grants at an enormous pace. Clearly, that is the model which is being chosen here in Canada as well. For $60 million net, Boeing is taking over de Havilland, despite the fact that de Havilland has received $200 million in advances from the Government just in the course of the last nine months, according to its most recent quarterly statement. Thus, for $60 million, Boeing receives an entity into which we have put $200 million just in the course of the last few months.
Boeing says that it will develop the new 50-seat version of the Dash-8 and expects it to qualify for repayable support under the Defence Industry Productivity Program. It interests me that an aircraft which I presume, and presumed, is to be used for commercial purposes will be financed by the Government of Canada under the DIPP. I suggest that is evidence that Boeing has said to the Conservative Government: "Look, if you guys and gals want to carry out your privatization and want some evidence that you can take around and show that privatization is a great thing, then give us access to the Defence Industry Productivity Program, despite the fact that what we are producing is a commercial aircraft for the civilian market".
The promises which have been made are vague and there is no guarantee that they can and will be enforced. It is said that de Havilland will keep its capacity for R and D, that it will be maintained and enhanced. How? It has been said that de Havilland will seek to increase the sale of Canadian content with respect to its products. How can that occur? There are no enforcement mechanisms in place.
Boeing has indicated publicly, and I think perhaps we can take the commitment seriously, that it will seek to develop the
