subsubtopic: JAMES BAY CREE AND NASKAPI SELF-GOVERNMENT-NEGOTIATION OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one and one-half years ago the House of Commons passed the Cree-Naskapi Act which was the first Indian self-government Act in our country. The Act fulfilled an obligation of the federal Government under the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, the first modern land claims settlement in Canada, an agreement, it should be noted, which is now constitutionalized.
For the past one and one-half years the James Bay Cree and Naskapi have been exercising self-government in their own communities and on their lands. At this time, however, there is a looming danger that this bold move forward may be sabo-

December 3, 1985
taged by a failure of the Government, backed by the Department of Indian Affairs, to live up to the financial commitments which accompanied the Act.
The Cree, the Naskapi, and a Minister of the Crown, the previous Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, signed a statement of understanding which allowed for annual adjustments of the grants to operate the self-government institutions. Rather than meaningful negotiations, there is now picayune quibbling and a concerted effort by the Government to wiggle and squeeze out of these commitments, rather than to honour them.
I plead with the Government. Do not hinder Indian self-government. Face up to your obligations. Proceed on the basis of good faith. Cease your efforts to frustrate the process.

subtopic: IMPACT OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX EXEMPTION
IMPACT OF CAPITAL GAINS TAX EXEMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within a very short time millions of Canadians will once again be asked to fill out their income tax forms. For most, this is an annual nightmare. The convoluted goobledygook of the income tax form is about as decipherable to the ordinary Canadian as are Egyptian hieroglyphics. The latest batch of amendments which the Government has brought forward will only add to the complexity and unfairness of the current system. None of these proposals is more of a boondoggle for the rich than the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption. Recently it was reported that:
The exemption will have a disastrous effect structurally on the tax system. Its scope is too broad . .. Practitioners fail to see how tax-free capital gains on the disposition of jewelry, summer cottages, or Florida condominiums provide much benefit for the economy.
Who am I quoting Mr. Speaker? A member of the New Democratic Party? No. The President of the National AntiPoverty Organization? No. I am quoting Mr. William Lawlor, national tax partner with Ernst & Whinney, former official in the tax policy division of the Department of Finance and a technical adviser to the Conservative Task Force on Revenue Canada.
Mr. Lawlor is hardly a radical, but you do not have to be a radical to understand that this tax break is unfair. When will the Government realize that shovelling more money into the pockets of the wealthy cannot substitute for a well planned, realistic approach to get Canada working again?

subtopic: SALE OF DE HAVILLAND-FULFILLMENT OF GOVERNMENT PROMISE
SALE OF DE HAVILLAND-FULFILLMENT OF GOVERNMENT PROMISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government has acted wisely in the sale of the de
Flavilland Company to Boeing. One of our campaign pledges was to privatize certain Crown corporations. More than $800 million of taxpayers' money was poured into this company over the years by Liberal Governments.
The Canadian content provision will create thousands of jobs for Canadians. The Government has taken a realistic and prudent step in moving de Havilland into the mainstream of world aircraft production.
It has long been clear that a successful aircraft industry must operate in a context of world marketing, sales and distribution organizations, and this will now be provided for de Havilland through the Boeing connection. At the same time the Government has taken steps to preserve Canadian expertise and enhance research and development at de Havilland.
The Boeing deal means the survival of de Havilland as a viable Canadian operation. It means the preservation of thousands of Canadian jobs and relief to the taxpayer from a huge and burdensome debt load. It should be praised, not criticized.

Mr. Speaker, the New Brunswick Federation of Home and School Associations has expressed to me its very great and valid concern about the violent and sexually explicit lyrics in today's so-called music.
My problem, and I suspect it is shared by many parents and grandparents, is that this garbage which passes for music is so atrocious that not only do we not pay attention to the words, we do not listen to it, period. However, it is time we did. It is time we listened to the smut coming across the air waves, songs like Darling Nikki, which I understand is about a girl who masturbates with a magazine: or another song called 10 Seconds to Love, about oral sex in an elevator; songs that promote not just rape, torture and rebellion, but even suicide among youth.
Over the weekend I heard Anne Murray, a Canadian superstar in the music industry, decry the lyrics of these songs, saying she does not listen to them and would not degrade herself by singing them.
I bring this to the attention of the House not to shock, although it is shocking, but to plead for a reaction to this moral degradation of our children by entertainers whose credo is that sex and violence sells. If this be culture, it is not Canadian culture. This call to arms was initiated by concerned parents and educators. Should we choose to ignore it, we do so at our peril.

Hear, hear!
December 3, 1985

FUNDING OF SASKATCHEWAN INDIANS' LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES

SALE OF DE HAVILLAND AIRCRAFT LTD. TO BOEING COMPANY

subtopic: SALE OF CANADIAN ARSENALS LTD.-REFUSAL OF SECOND BID
SALE OF CANADIAN ARSENALS LTD.-REFUSAL OF SECOND BID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while much attention has been directed toward yesterday's announcement of the sale of de Havilland by the federal Government, another Crown corporation was also sold yesterday. In this case it was not the money the Government threw out the window but jobs and investment for two provinces, Quebec and Nova Scotia, that need economic help of every kind.
Canadian Arsenals Ltd. was sold for $92.2 million. However, in its rush to sell the company, the Government of Canada dismissed another bid with a much more advantageous package of economic benefits. International Defence Products offered to purchase Canadian Arsenals Ltd. for a total price of $40 million. However, its package also included a promise that, in the first 12 months, 80 new full-time jobs in Quebec would be created, increasing personal incomes by $5 million, and that 130 new full-time jobs would be created in Nova Scotia, increasing personal income there by $31 million. There would be a $38 million expansion of existing facilities in Quebec, and a new brass mill and two modern plants would be established in Cape Breton, worth $100 million. The jobs would be permanent and pay an average of $25,000 per worker.
It was a total of $214 million in economic benefits to Canada and 200 well paying permanent jobs that the Government had a chance to create, yet it turned its back on the unemployed. They are the type of jobs that the Government promised my province and the Province of Quebec.

subtopic: SALE OF DE HAVILLAND AND CANADIAN ARSENALS LTD.- FULLFILMENT OF ELECTION COMMITMENT
SALE OF DE HAVILLAND AND CANADIAN ARSENALS LTD.- FULLFILMENT OF ELECTION COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to congratulate the Government on yesterday's announcement of the sale of two more Crown corporations, de Havilland Aircraft of Canada and Canadian Arsenals Ltd.
This is another step on the road to economic recovery and improving government management which we began just over one year ago.
In his Budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a task force to privatize or dissolve Crown corporations which no longer fulfil a specific public policy purpose. Previous announcements have been made regarding the sale or winding up of Northern Transportation Company Limited, the Canada Development Corporation, Canagrex, Loto Canada,
the Canadian Sports Pool Corporation, the Canada Museums Construction Corporation, and others.
Yesterday's announcement is particularly notable for the sale of de Havilland for $155 million. During the past 10 years de Havilland gobbled up $700 million of taxpayers' money. For the first nine months of this year the corporation had a loss of $55 million. Through this sale we are keeping a major promise to the Canadian people to take responsible action with regard to Crown corporations.
We were able to recognize a good deal when we saw one, something the previous Government failed to do, as well as relieve the taxpayers of a burden they have been carrying. The people of Canada recognize that it takes time to ensure that the deals we are negotiating are the best ones for Canada. They realize that the Government, as each day goes by, is making good on its commitment to good management and to stimulation of economic growth through the private sector.
These sales are a prime example of this administration, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), fulfilling another election commitment.

Mr. Speaker, I call on the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) to take action on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway pensioners who have lost their rail travel passes, a right they have had for generations.
There are many Members of the House who have protested this disgraceful unilateral action by the CPR toward former employees who have served it loyally. Some Members have also noted that the replacement health benefits do little for retirees in provinces with good provincial health plans, and that they actually interfere with the Blue Cross supplementary plan.
What Members may not know is that the Minister of Labour has stopped this issue from being heard as a grievance by the Canada Labour Relations Board as requested by the railway shopcraft unions.
Rather than give his approval for a hearing, the Minister instead sat on the application for two months while the passes expired, and then appointed his own investigator, which has further delayed any resolution.
The railway unions are still prepared to take the case of the CPR retirees to the CLRB. What is needed is approval from the Minister of Labour. Is the Minister prepared to act so that the case can be heard? Or is he, by his actions to date, only underlining the feelings of so many CP pensioners, namely, that justice delayed is justice denied?
December 3, 1985

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-ROLE OF PROVINCIAL PREMIERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a fairly direct question for the Prime Minister. It arises out of his agreement with the provincial First Ministers in Halifax. That agreement purported to allow full provincial participation in the negotiations with the United States on free trade. Does this mean that the provincial Premiers now have an effective veto over the negotiations with the United States?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-ROLE OF PROVINCIAL PREMIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the document which guides this is a matter of public record. It says that it is a preparatory phase and that during the preparatory phase the provinces agree with the federal Government, without in any way contesting the primacy of the federal Government, which remains unchallenged and undiminished, that we very much want intimate consultation to develop a strategy that will be beneficial to the provinces and to the country. To this end we have agreed upon a document, the four modalities of which are set forward in writing. It says that during the 90-day period, among other things, the preparatory work should include the determination of how best to give effect to the principle of full participation in the subsequent phases of the negotiation. That is what it is all about.
We very much want the provinces involved in the process, in the definition of the objectives and in the manner in which we do this as a nation. We think it is vital that we have their participation. We have actively sought it, and we welcome it.
Oral Questions
In the next 90 days we will deal with the manner in which it is secured.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course that is not the interpretation placed upon the agreement by the provincial Premiers. Premier David Peterson, at the end of the conference, said: "The bottom line is the negotiating team will take instructions from the First Ministers. That is where it is, and the final authority rests with the First Ministers". Donald Getty, the Premier of Alberta, said: "The negotiating team becomes our team". If those interpretations were placed on the agreement by the First Ministers at the conclusion of the conference-and 1 gather they were made in the presence of the Prime Minister-why did he not take issue with those statements and declare the federal position?

Mr. Speaker, because the federal position is the position which was agreed upon unanimously by the federal Government and the provinces, and reflected in this document. That is what it is all about. We agreed in a formal manner on the phases and the manner in which this would be developed. It was agreed upon with the provinces.
This is the first time we have engaged in this kind of negotiation. It is new to us. It is new to the provinces. We would never atttempt to bring home a deal which was not in the best interests of the provinces or one which did not enhance the prosperity of all Canadians. There is absolutely no reason for us even to contemplate that. This is the manner, the formal agreement between the provinces and the federal Government, whereby we set out the parameters and the modalities for achieving that objective. I think, in a federal state, that that is the proper way of doing it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has allowed a serious misinterpretation to arise on the part of the provincial Premiers. Obviously they feel that they have a full, direct, equal partnership in the negotiations and a veto over the negotiations. Is it to that the Prime Minister is agreeing? Is that what he is saying? This side of the House can agree with consultation, but we want to know what the definition of full provincial participation really means.
Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend put aside his negativism for a second and read the document, he might find out.

Hear, hear!

December 3, 1985
Oral Questions
We know the Liberal Party is against everything because it stands for nothing. It is just against. We know what it is against, but we do not know what it is for.
You're falling, Brian.

The answer is precisely in the document. That is what it is all about. I invite my right hon. friend to take a second to read the document which says that this preparatory work should include the determination of how best to give effect to the principle of full provincial participation in subsequent phases of the negotiations.
Ambassador Reisman, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister for International Trade will begin tomorrow their 90-day consultations with the provinces to produce the kinds of agreements that we hope will make absolutely redundant any reference to negativism and vetoes. We are not going to bring back anything that will be vetoed. We are going to make a good deal for Canada and all the provinces.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. It is about yesterday's sell-out of de Havilland. Last December I asked for the assurance that Investment Canada would be able to review any takeover of de Havilland before it became final. I was told by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion that it would not. He said: "Surely to suggest that Investment Canada should have a review in addition to cabinet review and that which would take place in this House is totally unnecessary". Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to participate in this very important debate, particularly as it relates to an indusry which I believe is important to all Canadians. Approximately a year ago, shortly after the federal election, the Conservative Government, with great haste, announced to the Parliament and the people of Canada its desire and intention to sell a number of Canadian-owned Crown corporations. One corporation which was talked about at great length was de Havilland of Canada Limited. In fact, in numerous utterances in this House, in press releases, and in various statements made by Ministers of the Crown the Government's desire to unload this Canadian Crown corporation was emphasized. However, there were no restrictions or limitations as to who might be the purchaser of this Crown corporation.
The sale price of $155 million for this particular Crown corporation is worth noting and deserves careful consideration by all Members of Parliament. Boeing will pay $155 million; $90 million in cash and $65 million in a note repayable over 15 years. There are some other facts which I think ought to be read into the record. For each $5 million of new orders to Canadian suppliers $1 million will be cut from the amount which is outstanding. Second, Ottawa will pay part of any increases in de Havilland's liability insurance for all its planes now flying. This can cut the purchase price by some $30 million according to the Chairman of the CDIC.
In addition, Boeing will be allowed to carry forward de Havilland's losses for tax purposes but has agreed to use the benefit only for lending moneys to Canadian buyers of de Havilland's planes. This can cut the purchase price by $400 million according to the Chairman of a competitor, Rimgate. Boeing will pay a royalty of a specified amount on all sales of models developed by de Havilland. Finally, Boeing will benefit from all available federal programs including the loans the Government now provides to support sales of Dash-7s and Dash-8s.
That is the sale price, Mr. Speaker. On one side of the ledger there is $155 million and on the other side the Government of Canada is investing in excess of $700 million. Its assets today at market value would be in excess of $300 million, plus the added features which were attached to the agreement in small print with regard to the benefits under the Income Tax Act and the carrying forward of certain liabilities thereto. The sale price is $155 million. It can be argued and

substantiated that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has now put Canada up for sale and the price is a meagre $155 million for this Crown corporation.
There was an argument advanced many months ago by members of the Opposition about prudent and competent managers of the economy. The evidence which has been adduced thus far does not prove to a reasonable individual that it would be prudent and competent for Canadians to be involved in this deal. Perhaps at some time in the near future the memorandum of understanding signed by de Havilland and Boeing will clarify for Members of Parliament and the Canadian people exactly what the bargaining position of the Government of Canada was with relation to this particular subject matter.
de Havilland is a good company. It has a world product mandate. Why would a multinational corporation like Boeing not want to pick up de Havilland for $155 million? Those in the private sector would say that this is the private sector at its best, it is cherry picking. They take that which is the best and leave that which is not. They cannot lose in this deal, Mr. Speaker, de Havilland will build the Dash-7 and Dash-8. Why else would Boeing want to buy this particular company? Boeing knows a quality product even if the Government of Canada does not.
With the deregulation of the airline industry the Dash-7 and Dash-8, short take off and landing aircraft, are about to come into their own displacing many jets built by Boeing. It only makes sense that an American company would buy out the competition. To date de Havilland has 117 orders for its Dash-8 aircraft. The Government allowed the Canadian people to accept all the risk over the past ten years and has now handed an American company the opportunity for profits which rightly belong, not to the Government of Canada, but to the people of Canada.
This is a tragedy in that it can be argued successfully that it is comparable to the 1959 Avro Arrow situation. There was a large Conservative majority Government involved in that particular decision which affected Canadian industry. Canadians saw a wealth of technology along with individuals with ideas and expertise migrate to the United States, thus becoming the real substance behind the American thrust to have a man on the moon. I do not know where this trip will lead us, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that the selling of de Havilland at this point in time without the necessary qualifications is not good for Canada. It is not good for the workers and it is certainly not good for the Canadian economy.
What about consultation, Mr. Speaker? In the Throne Speech, the budget, and subsequent speeches by Members opposite, we heard about consultation. Did the Government consult with the United Auto Workers? Did the Government do, as the Prime Minister would say, the honourable thing by consulting with the workers involved? No, it did not.
Did the Government consult with the Ontario Government? According to Premier Peterson's office, the Government of
Ontario has received two communications from the Government of Canada concerning the de Havilland takeover. One was an acknowledgement of a request made by the Government of Ontario well over a year ago to be consulted on the possibility of a de Havilland sale. I regret to report that the second one occurred last Friday at the First Ministers' Conference in Halifax. At that time, officials of the Ontario Government were told that the deed was done.
What happened to the claim of the Prime Minister that co-operative federalism is here? Why was there no meaningful consultation with the Ontario Government? Why was there no consultation with the United Auto Workers? The critics will argue that it was to provide a sweetheart deal to Boeing. There was no consultation because the Government wanted to circumvent every possible concern and objection regarding this particular transfer so that it could be put in the hands of Boeing.
There was a press conference at which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) made a statement. He talked about a memorandum of understanding. Where is that memorandum of understanding? For a time, the President of the Treasury Board argued in the House that jobs would be increased in de Havilland. Where are the figures? Where is the documentation which would allow Canadians to view for themselves the investment intentions of Boeing? We have seen no memorandum of understanding.
Of course, Government Members have the answers. They say that there are a few details yet to be decided upon and once they are decided upon they will table the document. It may be many, many months before the people of Canada will really know what has transpired. Then, unfortunately, it will be too late.
During Question Period today and in the speeches of Hon. Members who have preceded me, there has been mention of job guarantees. Approximately 4,500 Canadians are employed with de Havilland. There has been not one word in the documents provided by the Minister on jobs guarantees. The tragedy of that is that the Government has demonstrated in other areas of the Canadian economy-I will not talk about the banks, the multinational oil companies or anything of that nature-that it does not have the business acumen or prudence required to assure that workers in Canada will be protected as a result of this takeover.
It is very evident that in this particular agreement between de Havilland and Boeing, nothing has been mentioned about job guarantees. I stand to be corrected on this and 1 hope I can be corrected on it. However, until such time as 1 see the memorandum of understanding and the documents that have been exchanged by the two companies, I must conclude the very obvious: there are no job guarantees for Canadians in the transfer of de Havilland to Boeing.
What about the technology transfer? Boeing has recognized that Canadians have developed a superb technology, a technology which will be able to take advantage of a market which I believe, though I am not an expert, will open up significantly in the next number of years. We have provided an American
December 3, 1985

company with a certain amount of goodwill. The Prime Minister has said that Canada is open for business. Ele just sold it right off for a song.
What about research and development? Were any financial guarantees included in the documents that were provided? No, Mr. Speaker. Was there mention made of the percentage of research and development that would have to be done in Canada? No, there was none whatsoever. There has been no financial commitment and no commitment with regard to the percentage of research and development that ought to be done in Canada by Canadians for Canadians.
The argument that some of us have made and will continue to make is that we are transferring to the United States technology, individuals and brainpower without even protecting here in Canada something that we have developed and on which we have spent millions of millions of taxpayers' dollars. I believe that is shameful.
Perhaps Members of Parliament are asking of the Government something that it is impossible for it to do. Perhaps this request of Government Members and particularly the Cabinet is something with which they cannot comply. Perhaps other countries in the world cannot restrict foreign control. In the United States Federal Aviation Act of 1958, 49 U.S. Code, Section 1301, Subsections 3 and 16 indicate that Boeing is allowed to do something in Canada that it is not allowed to do in the United States. Boeing is classfied as being vital to the aviation sector of the American economy and consequently is not allowed to sell any more than 25 per cent of its interests to a foreign Government. What happens in Canada? The Prime Minister, that great vocalist, travels to Washington and New York, sings a song for the President of the United States and tells Boeing to come on over to get 100 per cent of a Canadian Crown corporation without any restrictions whatsoever. How are Canadians protected from this takeover? There is not one iota of protection.
Neither the Prime Minister, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) nor the President of the Treasury Board have placed Canadian interests first. What we are pointing out to Government Members is not something which is completely alien to all western democracies. In the United States, there are restrictions on industries that are vital to the economy. I suggest that this particular sector of the Canadian economy is vital and that there ought to have been restrictions in place with regard to the selling of de Havilland to the Boeing Corporation.
The Government has carried on in such a way that one cannot believe what it says any longer. The Prime Minister says one thing and does the opposite. He reassures Canadians, yet he taketh away. In New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, he said that we ought to increase transfer payments. He told the First Ministers that he did not say that and that he meant something else. On August 17, 1984 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised to turn Canadair Limited and de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Ltd. into separate Crown corporations to develop new products in the aerospace industry. That is what the Minister of Finance said with a great deal of integrity.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak against the motion which is before the House today and to support the sale of de Havilland. I am fortunate that there are several aerospace manufacturers in my riding of Winnipeg-St. James, such companies as Bristol Aerospace, Standard Aero and Boeing of Winnipeg. I can tell you, Sir, that, as a professional engineer, 1 am also concerned that the technology developed in Canada within the aerospace industry be preserved and expanded. 1 am confident that with the purchase of de Havilland by Boeing, we will see that objective achieved.
I found it interesting this morning when the Leader of the New Democratic Party rose to speak about a sale of a Crown corporation. In fact, if you were in the House at that time, Mr. Speaker, you would have heard me ask a question with regard to what his stance was in Manitoba because 1 feel it is important that Hon. Members who are not from Manitoba recognize what the policy of the New Democratic Party in Manitoba is as compared to the policy of the same Party in the House of Commons. As we all know, the basic social philosophy of the New Democratic Party is that the Government should own businesses and employ people. It is odd that when that Party is in Opposition it expounds on how good companies are which are Government owned and how they are useful to social programs. However, I would like to cite my experiences in Manitoba with respect to Crown owned corporations when we had a Schreyer Government as well as a Howard Pawley Government.
We had experiences with Saunders aircraft which cost the taxpayers of Manitoba S40 million before the then Ed Schreyer Government decided it should close it down, realizing that the taxpayers of Manitoba had supported this Crown corporation to the fullest extent it could. That amount of money does not sound as much as the $800 million we are talking about here, but when one considers Manitoba has a population of one million people, one can readily see it is an amount equivalent, in Canada as a whole, of $1 billion.
We have had bad experiences in Manitoba with Chinese food manufacturers which the Government owned and then closed down. What has happened now is that the NDP Government in Manitoba has done a complete flip in its philosophy that Government should have Crown-owned corporations when it comes to Flyer Industries. Flyer Industries is a manufacturer of buses. I would like to quote what the present Government of Manitoba has said. In June of this year Hon. Eugene Kostyra, the Minister who is responsible for Crown corporations, made a statement in committee that he was going to sell Flyer Industries this year and if he did not, he would close it down. But where was the Minister of the NDP Government last month? He was in the Netherlands trying to

sell Flyer Industries, a Crown corporation, to a foreign company. The NDP opposition in the House of Commons have made a complete about-face of 180 degrees. It wants to retain a Crown corporation. It is protesting that we should not sell de Havilland to private industry, or what it calls a "multinational".
1 would ask Hon. Members of the Manitoba-NDP caucus at the federal level if they have talked to their colleagues in Manitoba. What has been said about selling Flyer Industries? Have they raised any objections to this, particularly the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie)? Flyer Industries is right in his riding. Those Hon. Members rise and protest that we are doing the wrong thing when in Manitoba their own NDP Government is trying to do the same thing we are doing.
I can tell you why, Mr. Speaker. It is because of the fact that when a Party becomes the Government it finds all of a sudden it cannot afford the haemorrhaging of taxpayers' money which Crown corporations cause. 1 call it "haemorrhaging" because that is exactly what it is. I sat around a Cabinet table in Manitoba arguing for money for mental rehabilitation programs. We were refused. We were told the Government had to put the money into the support of Flyer Industries or some other Crown corporations. That is exactly what is happening here. The taxpayers' money which is going to these Crown corporations is being stolen from these other programs which are needed by our taxpayers.
I hope that the New Democratic Party will recognize that we are in no different position from their colleagues in Manitoba who are trying to sell Flyer Industries. The haemorrhaging has to be stopped. How long can we continue to pump millions and millions of dollars into these particular Crown corporations only to see them lose money?
What really hurts in any industry such as Flyer Industries in Manitoba is the fact that when the manufacturer makes a product which is sold outside its provincial boundaries or its country, and if it is being sold at a loss, the taxpayers of that province or the country subsidize the transit systems in other places such as Chicago and San Francisco. Every time Flyer Industries sells a bus, it gives a $92,000 contribution to one of those transit companies. I do not know what the figure is when de Havilland sells an aeroplane, but, obviously, if we have pumped $800 million into that company and it has had a $76 million loss last year and has already lost $55 million this year, when we export its product, we are subsidizing an airline industry in another part of the world. 1 say that it is time to stop and the sale to Boeing will stop that because Boeing will be responsible for any losses.
When it is argued that Boeing will get all of the grants, it can be argued that de Havilland gets all those grants now. Nothing has changed except that de Havilland has a $55 million loss this year which will be the responsibility of Boeing next year. 1 believed that should be drawn to the attention of the Opposition because it will not accept the fact that the Boeing company will pick up any losses which occur.

I would like to comment on Boeing Winnipeg because I think it is important to explain to the House of Commons why I have confidence that Boeing will keep its word. My acquaintance with Boeing goes back some 15 years. I was on the St. James Assiniboia Council at the time when Boeing approached us and said it would like to locate in our city. The City of St. James sold Boeing 126 acres of prime industrial land in a west end industrial area. It was the first to go in there. We were naturally concerned about a company from the United States perhaps taking advantage of Canadians. We were concerned that it would perhaps purchase 126 acres and when it got the acreage it would subdivide it, sell it and make a profit and then pay for its buildings and so on. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Boeing has not done that. Boeing in Winnipeg developed a plant which employed 57 people in 1971. It expanded to employ 300 employees by 1973. It then continued to expand its technology in the space industry and is now presently employing 650 people. I could not believe what I heard yesterday in the press conference of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I would think that a former Minister of Transport would know what is happening in his City of Winnipeg. He made the statement that Boeing makes bathtubs. Do you know when Boeing stopped making bathtubs? Two years ago. That is how up-to-date the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry is on what is happening in the transportation industry in Winnipeg.
At one time there was no space technology, no manufacturing of specialized plastic and fibreglass components for this industry in Winnipeg. Boeing developed that technology and brought it to Canada. That plant is now supplying components for the 757 and 767 Boeing aircraft. Second generation aircraft components are being built in Winnipeg using technology developed in Canada with the guidance of that company's U.S. engineering department. It is also developing specialized tooling and fabrication. The company is doing work on satellites. The Opposition is talking about a flow of technology out of Canada but I suggest that there will be a growth of technology in Canada. I am quite confident about that.
The Hon. Member left the impression that all Boeing did was build bathtubs. He downgraded a very important industry in Winnipeg and a very good corporate citizen. To give an idea of the kind of employer they are, there are about 1,065 Canadians working for Boeing in Canada. 1 had a chance to talk to the president of Boeing this morning. I asked him how many Americans his company employed to run the show in Canada. His answer? Zero. They are all Canadians, Canadian engineers and workers. The Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broad-bent) talked about wrapping the stars and stripes around de Havilland. However, everyone who works for Boeing in Canada is a Canadian. He should check his facts before he starts making statements like that. There has also been all this talk about multinationals. Do you know where Boeing has its factories? In the United States and Canada. That is all. I did not know that a multinational operated in only two countries. What we are getting with Boeing is a corporate citizen which
is interested in Canada and Canadians. To give an example, the unused part of their plant site in Winnipeg contains a herd of deer which the company feeds all year round. The company also allows its employees to have garden plots at the plant if they want to make use of them. This is the kind of corporate citizen which has bought de Havilland.
The last speaker made a statement with regard to the quality of the product they produce. I think we all agree that de Havilland makes several damn good aircraft. However, you can make the best pump or the best aircraft in the world but if you do not have the marketing ability, you end up with a yard full of pumps or a hangar full of aircraft. That is what happened to Saunders Aircraft. It did not have a world-wide marketing ability. The aircraft industry is a very unique industry. Millions and millions of dollars are involved when buying a fleet of aircraft, whether it be two, three or whatever. You expect to get a least 25 or 30 years life out of an aircraft. You want the parts to be available when you need them. You want the guarantees when you need them. Boeing brings that to de Havilland. de Havilland has the product quality and Boeing has a world-wide reputation for providing a guaranteed product and making sure parts are always available.
When Boeing expanded its plant in Winnipeg in 1979, I asked the then vice-president what the value was of the company's total sales of aircraft world-wide. His answer was $8.3 billion. That tells me that if we get Boeing operating de Havilland it will apply its expertise to reduce the cost of manufacturing. It will apply its marketing ability and supply the confidence the buyer wants. We will see an excellent relationship between these two companies. I am confident that the technology will stay in Canada and grow. I am confident the other Boeing plants in Canada will expand as well. We will have a wider market and more jobs. Our main objective is to have sound stable jobs in this industry and further expansion of technological development. For those reasons I am opposed to the motion and I support the sale of de Havilland.

Member was listening to my comments earlier but my experience with Boeing in Winnipeg shows that the reverse is true. That company kept investing money in our community and in the Province of Manitoba. It has expanded the job population. It has not transferred the engineers to Boeing in Seattle. It has brought technology here and has developed new technology in tooling to handle the new second generation aircraft. I am basing my comments on what I have seen in Winnipeg. I cannot comment

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) is relying on good intentions and the record of the company. Mr. Speaker, 1 must say that 1 am tempted to begin by talking about socialist Chinese food in Winnipeg. It seems to weigh heavily on the mind of my colleague across the aisle.
I believe the time of the House would be more valuably taken by focusing on the issue itself, which is not whether there are good subsidiaries. I can say quite frankly that there are some excellent foreign subsidiaries in my constituency which contribute greatly to this country. I have just written a letter of welcome to one of those subsidiaries which we have been able to persuade to come from West Germany to make a contribution to economic development in Essex-Windsor.
The question we are considering is whether it makes sense to be selling good, solid technologically dynamic Canadian companies, when we already have so few in our economy, especially at a giveaway price which will eventually be an expense to taxpayers. The Government will have to face this question when it goes back to the electorate in three years. It will have to face the fact that there is a commitment in this country to Canadianization of the economy.
I have indicated to the House before that statistics from polling undertaken by Decima Research Ltd. indicates clearly that 85 per cent of Canadians want to see legislation to encourage greater Canadian ownership of industry. They want to see a greater presence of Canadians in the business community, rather than a sell-out of those flagships of Canadian industrial progress which already exist.
However, that is exactly what has taken place under the Conservative Government. Instead of Canadianization of our economy, the Government clearly believes in its Americanization. I had hoped that the Government's record in its first six months of office would have been an aberration about which it would have some shame. Rather, it has continued to revel in the fact that it is creating a more Americanized and continentalized economy in which Canada is bound to become the appendage or ignored part of a North American economy that has been integrated by free trade and dominated by American corporations.
Again and again we have seen Ministers rise in the House to glorify the fact that good, solid Canadian corporations, some from the private sector and some from the public sector, are slipping into the hands of the United States. They have not apologized. They have not said that they were sorry that this was happening or that they did what they could to make things come together but it just did not work. Instead they have glorified it. The Americanization of the Canadian economy, under the direction of the Conservative Party, goes on in abject shame.
Let us look at what has happened. For instance, Mitel was sold to foreigners. In the case of White Farm, small-scaled, high-powered Canadian entrepreneurs in the private sector were trying to get it going in Brantford. We saw it sold out and given up by the Government. A workers' co-operative in Hamilton looked to Canadian Porcelain, a small company, to make a contribution to that community. It was sold out. That time it was sold out to the U.S. company which had put it in trouble in the first place by dumping into the country through systems of unfair trade. Also we had the case of Black & Decker, as well as the great epitome of American capitalization, the takeover of CGE in Barrie. The factory was shut down within a year. It shifted its operations, cut its employment and turned factories, which had contributed hundreds of jobs to people in Barrie for a generation, into ghost town warehouses. Also we had the fiasco with the Canada Development Corporation. Through all kinds of back-handed manoeuvres and actions before the House even had a chance to consider the matter, the Government allowed 25 per cent of a company which was important to our future to be sold to the United States. We have had no action on Prentice-Hall, a case which has been before us for over a year now. Canadian publishers want to purchase the company. They do not want to turn it into a socialist enterprise, God help us. They want to turn it into a privately held Canadian company which will contribute to the country. Again the Government has refused to move.
The black list or the sad story of Americanization under the Government goes on and on, with the last sorry story added to it now of de Havilland, a good and dynamic company, a company with exciting new products which it is succeeding in selling throughout the world. Now that company is to become one more trophy in the corporate shareholding list of the Boeing Corporation with its billions of dollars in sales, de Ha-
December 3, 1985

villand today, Canadair next, and the Canadian aircraft industry, as a Canadian-owned, Canadian-controlled industry with a sense of Canadian potential, will in fact go down the drain. It will be abandoned by the Government as it has abandoned so much of the key sectors of the economy to United States capital over the last 14 months.
It is especially dangerous to see this happening to the high-tech sectors of our economy. We as a country are not embarrassed by our riches in the high-tech sector. We do not have masses of Canadian-controlled companies making contributions and selling exports in that sector. We as a country have problems because we are small, because the risks are great and because the costs are high to create high-tech innovations. Yet, we have had our success stories. We have had our Mitels, our Northern Telecoms, and our de Havil-lands. Far too often the Government permits companies such as those to go down the drain, so far as being part of a Canadian core for high-technology growth in the future.
I should like to present to the House a segment of the report of the Ontario Government about what companies could make it under free trade. It indicates quite clearly that one sector which can make it under free trade, despite the intense competition it will have to face with the United States, could be our aircraft and aircraft parts manufacturers.
I will give the House a sense of how superbly that sector has done in terms of international trade. International trade is crucial for the future. In 1978, that sector of our economy in Ontario ran a trade deficit. Its exports amounted to about $174 million and its imports about $219 million. By 1984, its exports were up to $548 million, while its imports ran at $383 million. It is a success story built upon the very risks and the new product developments which have characterized de Havil-land, which should characterize de Havilland in the future and which would characterize it if it remained a Canadian company able to make its contribution to the economy.
It is tough. One cannot start a high-tech company overnight. It takes heavy investment. It takes high risks. It takes longtime horizons. In the case of de Havilland, it has taken over $800 million to put together two excellent, highly-innovative, new pieces of technology which are among the best in the world in their class-the Dash-7 and the Dash-8. Now, in 1985, as December is upon us, here comes Santa Claus to give it away. Here it comes, gift-wrapped in nice tinsel paper with a bright red or perhaps blue maple leaf on it, to be placed under the corporate Christmas tree of the Boeing Corporation, to be given away as a gift. It is the kind of gift which I used to receive as a child from my grandfather. I am sure that many Hon. Members in the Chamber received such gifts. It was a gift which not only included the gift itself but, when it was opened, there was $2 or $5 in it; a gift which gives something and some money as well.
This is a super grandpa's gift to the Boeing Corporation. It is a gift described by Boeing Corporation as costing no more than the price of one 747 aircraft. It is the gift of a company
Supply
that is making excellent operating profits. There have been some mis-statements made in this debate, but the fact of the matter is that income from operations of de Havilland for 1985 was almost $18 million in positive surplus. That is up from approximately $6 million the year before, so there has been a huge increase in operating profits. That increase was due to an increase from 19 to 27 in the number of planes sold. Boeing tells us that it expects to continue with this increase in operating profits. By the time the costs for research and development for the Dash-8 start to be paid off in a year or two the company is going to be making over-all profits rather than just operating profits.
There is money tucked into every possible little pocket of this magnificent gift. Let me list for the House some of the gift-wrapped envelopes of taxpayers' money which are included in this Christmas gift to Boeing Corporation. They get to defer $65 million of the sale price and probably will not have to pay it at all. That is not bad for Christmas, but that is just a start. Also included in the gift is the Crown's share of product liability insurance, worth $30 million and the development costs for the Dash-8 amounting to $65 million which will be paid by the taxpayers of the country and will go to the benefit of Boeing.
Surely it must make my back-bench colleagues in the Conservative Party, who care about fiscal rectitude, blush just a little bit to see this incredible, unjustified largesse to a foreign multinational company. Also included in the gift is export financing of $30 million to $40 million and, to top it off, a tax loss carry-forward of $400 million, not just to de Havilland but to all of Boeing in Canada. That is why the Winnipeg Boeing people are so pleased.
Do you realize what $400 million could do for the hard-pressed farmers of Essex County or the hard-pressed farmers of all of southern Ontario? Think what it could do for potential jobs of small business people in Quebec, northern Manitoba and the interior of British Columbia. That is the tax loss which is given. Santa Claus will continue down the path passing out these magnificent gifts and creating, not a fairy tale out of Jack and Jill, but a nightmare of Tory rule which we saw before with the Arrow in the 1950s and which we see now with de Havilland in the 1980s.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, these are tough issues. Building our industrial future is not easy. There are hard choices which we must make. We must start by telling the Government not to sell us out as a country, to stop giving us away to foreign firms and to stop doing it at the expense of the taxpayer of the country who is already so hard pressed that he and she deserve relief and the Christmas gifts rather than the Boeing Corporation of Seattle.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this chamber we have to get used to the use of hyperbole. A lot of exaggeration goes on on both sides. The Member who just spoke has certainly used his fair share and someone else's too when exaggerating in his speech. He used words like "abandoned" and said that the Government was letting companies like this "go down the drain". I guess the use of hyperbole is okay, but as a former professor he will know that over-use of hyperbole soon destroys the person using it. I will let that take care of itself. No one will believe him if he continues to use that kind of exaggeration.
He should know, as I am sure he does, that this year, next year, and the following year when these aircraft are made and sold around the world they will have a plate on them that says "Made in Canada". He makes it sound as though they are going to be made in the United States now. Does he realize that this will continue to be a Canadian product? In fairness, he should not try to make the people of Canada believe that
just because an American company has bought the company it is now going to be an American plane. As a matter of fact, it will be competing with American planes and will do very well with the kind of world market mandate which it has been given.
I would like to make one other point on the matter of accuracy. The Member went on to say that Boeing was going to be forgiven $65 million. In terms of accuracy and honesty, would it not be good to give the entire equation and tell the people that this is on a five-to-one ratio? For every $5 million that Boeing spends in the market-place across Canada in ancillary industries, whether or not it is for de Havilland, they will be forgiven $1 million. There is a multiplier in there. Would it not be only right and fair, when talking about a $65 million forgiveness, that he talk about the $300 million market which Boeing will have to develop in order to get that forgiveness?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Member for his question. I think it was Aneurin Beavan who once stated that words occasionally have to be a little bit wild to shake the unthinking. Frankly, as I look at this so-called deal, 1 think that it could only have been put together by people who were unthinking about the sense of potential benefit that could exist for our country by having our own well developed, expanding aircraft industry as opposed to letting it become an appendage of the U.S. aircraft industry. We can slice it different ways and we can use different words but the bottom line is that as a consequence of this move, de Havilland will become an appendage of a very much large U.S. aircraft company, a company which without question will shape the direction it takes in the future.
I believe the implications of this move throughout the world make an interesting point. A big part of our problem in attempting to sell export products to Southeast Asia, Africa, Latin America or other countries which I have visited has been that we do not have a reputation for making contributions to the world of high technology innovation. Frankly, by making de Havilland a division of Boeing Corporation, we will simply prove to those countries throughout the world that the image we already have is the correct image.
Regarding the question of the sale price, the point I made was that that $65 million was deferred. The Hon. Member is quite right in suggesting that the way to get forgiveness is by increasing purchases here in Canada, something which I think is perfectly appropriate. However, to begin by deferring a part of the sale price is taking the opposite tack to that which we as a Government would have taken and that is that we would tell the company to pay its money and make a commitment to buy a certain amount of its production needs here in Canada. It seems to me that in this case, we are saying that the actual price that will be paid by Boeing is only $90 million and we are saying that at the same time as all these other financial goodies are under the same Christmas tree.



December 3, 1985

1 know that the Hon. Member has a reputation of being concerned about the extravagance of Government expenditure.
I hope that he will take the occasion of this debate to look at these incredible potential taxpayer liabilities that attach to the sale of de Havilland of which the $65 million is just one and see to it that this taxpayer liability is reduced in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to comment on some of the point raised by the Hon. Member for Essex-Wind-sor (Mr. Langdon), who represents my neighbouring riding. First, I would point out that the $200 million that it would cost to keep the company going next year could very well be used by the farmers of Essex County and those across Canada and 1 hope that it will be.
When the Hon. Member began his speech, I thought for a moment that he was going to compliment us. He pointed out that there were some very good American corporate citizens in his riding. The major employers in his area are Chrysler and General Motors, both of which have proven to be very good corporate citizens. Gathering from the Hon. Member's own householder, the Government has probably given his riding more assistance than any other riding in the country in order to develop the high-tech industry in the Windsor area. The Hon. Member should be very thankful to the Conservative Government for doing that for his riding.
1 would like to ask the Hon. Member why he feels that Boeing is not a dynamic company. Does he not think that it is the world leader in aerodynamics and will inject into the Canadian economy more money than the Government could have put in over the next few years?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that 1 am pleased to hear that my householder is such a bestseller that it even penetrates other constituencies. Quite frankly, I am one of those Members who works very hard to get companies to move into my constituency and to make commitments to increase employment in the constituency. Our success record is something of which I am quite proud. It is, I think, a reflection of something that is true of New Democrats and that is that we are not, as we are sometimes painted to be, the foes of the private sector. speechtext: It is solemn and sober. There is no satisfaction taken by any Hon. Member on this side of the House at the deal that was struck by the Government. It is a deal that we know was propelled by the Draconian motives of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) who wishes to privatize Canadian Government activities. The way it has been done is stupid and ignorant. God, how awful this Government has become that it is so totally indifferent to the interests of the Canadian people and this industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
The fact that Tory Members are laughing about this only underlines just how hardened and calloused they have become toward what Canada is all about. 1 suppose they may be laughing out of embarrassment. They know that they are members of a Government which acquired office to see to the dismantling of Canada's sense of independence and integrity and its ability to provide a future that it will determine on its own. It is too bad that there is such insensitivity to those issues.
The fact is that this particular debate must be used to bring the lessons home so that Canadians will understand in the future what has happened here. The First thing Canadians must undersatnd is how poor a businessman the Government really is.
I attended a conference on Saturday at which a member of the Conservative caucus said that one of the great changes that took place as a result of the election of September 1984 was that the composition of the House of Commons has changed and that Conservatives now have a large representation by small business people. If 1 were John Bulloch or a representative of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business I would be ashamed of that. For all the so-called new business acumen, let us consider what they have done. Let us consider what kind of deal they have made. If one takes a look at the figures one will find that once again they have sold the store for nothing but fantasy and fond wishes. Today I said that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) was fortunate in that Boeing did not offer the Government the Brooklyn Bridge for de Havilland because he would have thought that was a good deal. He would have grabbed it at the first opportunity.
I would like to point out to Hon. Members the type of things which we must look at with respect to this particular negotiation. First, and I think this is a serious charge which 1 must register, the Government has been guilty of serious irregular business practices. These are practices which, under normal business operations, would not be countenanced by any proper auditor of accounting. In order to deliberately show that de Havilland was having heavy losses what the Government did was take the funds being used for development purposes in the new product lines and charged that amount against operating costs. Under normal business practices these charges are normally amortized over 15 or 20 years. Whenever any business
9094

December 3, 1985

makes a new investment over a period of time it puts it down on the books as a development cost. However, the Government, members of which are smart business people, charged the amount against operating costs. Therefore, when it comes time to sell an aeroplane the new owner will have virtually free and unfettered attachments to the cashflow because there will be no development costs. They have been written off as a result of the accounting practices of the Government.
However, there was a political purpose in this respect. Members of the Government were motivated because they wanted to put the books in front of the Canadian people in order to say: "Look, de Havilland is losing money. We had better show just how bad it is". Instead, they finagled and played the old accounting shell game. They moved forward what would be legitimate development investment expenditures and said that even last year with regard to a sale of $ 192 million de Havilland made only $11.1 million. The company was charged $78 million against its future investments. How can that be justified? What type of so-called smart business practice is that? It may be smart politics, although I do not think so, but it has nothing to do with honesty and integrity in terms of coming to grips with the issue of de Havilland.
One of the really great sights yesterday came about at the press conference held after the announcement of the sale. Someone asked the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) a question something like this: "You are selling this company for $150 million. What are its assets worth?" The Ministers went through their books and they fumbled their papers and looked in the reports. Finally, they had to say: "We don't know". Here were two Ministers of the Crown making a public announcement of great significance and they did not know the value of the assets. In terms of commercial value the land around the Downsview Airport in that part of Toronto is worth more than the amount received for the sale. If one were to talk to municipal officials in that municipality one would find out what could reasonably be expected in terms of the value of the land, to say nothing of the equipment, the capital and development costs and all the other assets which normally go into accounting in terms of the total value of a company.
These Ministers are out selling this company without even caring about what they are selling. They did not care what the value was because the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion wants to privatize. That is his religion. His theology is to privatize. It does not matter for what, what impact it will have or how it will influence the aerospace industry. He just wants to get rid of it. That is his answer.
I would like to set out another example of good business practices, as this Government likes to term it. The Government accepted a full share of the corporate liability and the insurance costs with respect to the aeroplanes. Boeing will have the value of all the assets and all the cashflow but the Canadian taxpayer gets stuck with the insurance costs and future liabilities. Is that not a brilliant stroke of negotiating skill? Does that not show an incredible sense of judgment? We will be stuck for the bill way down the line. Mr. Marshall was not too
sure about the figure but he thought it was around $30 million. Where is that reflected in the sale price? What did Boeing do to receive that kind of deal? I will bet Hon. Members there is not one other deal which Boeing has ever entered into in which it received this type of sweetheart arrangement.
In addition to taking the $90 million in cash and not the full $150 million, the Government said it is also prepared to continue giving grants and loans for the development of the Dash-8, for other research and for modernization of the plant. We are talking about another $300 million or $400 million of additional government money going into this project. As was asked today: "Where are the taxpayers represented?" They will not be represented on the Board of Directors. Will they have any equity? Will they receive anything in return? They will not receive a sou-not a cent.
When we talk about free trade with the United States it is no wonder we say: "God save this country if this is the Government negotiating the deal". It is no wonder we have some concerns when we see the silkful negotiating and bargaining which these wizards of commercial transactions are able to arrive at. The Government sells the company at a write-down price, takes on additional commitments and it receives no equity. As has been said, what we end up with in the result is the loss of any ability to set the direction or management in an area of crucial and vital interest in terms of the Canadian export market.
The Government sold this company just when it was beginning to make money. The company had spent several years investing in a new generation of aeroplanes. The atmosphere of deregulation around the world is creating a new market for commercial aircraft. Just as the taxpayers of Canada were about to realize a return on their investment what did the Tories do? They are so smart that they sold this company off before we could receive the return. That is a great tribute to their great business acumen.
Conservative Members in the House, in particular the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Minaker) and others, have said: "Don't worry about it. We have such a wonderful deal with Boeing and they are such a wonderful company that there is nothing to be concerned about". I would like to provide some commentary on that point. First, what is wrong with selling the company to an American multinational? Boeing is certainly a world-class company. It has a wonderful line of aeroplanes. However, to think that it will all of sudden play noblesse oblige with de Havilland is ridiculous.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James spoke about the Boeing factory in Winnipeg. I would like to tell Hon. Members another side to that story. When the building was first developed on grants from the federal Government the commitment then was for a world product mandate similar to what de Havilland was given with respect to fibreglass technology in terms of aeroplanes. However, along the way, in the late 1970s when the airline business began to go into a trough, somehow or other that commitment disappeared. At that time the ability of Boeing in Winnipeg to maintain an independent marketing line for aircraft technology in fibreglass somehow disappeared.
December 3, 1985

It ended up making a few spare parts. Do Hon. Members know what the company is making now? It is making bathtubs. This is Canada's great vault into the new high technology area. This is the new frontier that Boeing of Canada has established in Winnipeg. It is now making bathtubs, which is not a bad product. There is nothing wrong with bathtubs. After all, people have to wash. However, if Canadians think they bought a new frontier in high technology they may want to think again.

speechtext: Can they fly?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
We have never tried.
The fact of the matter is that it was a commitment of the Government.
I would like to point out some other facts with respect to the record. In front of me I have a wonderful article which appeared in The New York Times on September 8. It deals with the type of corporate citizen Boeing is in the United States. The company pleaded guilty to charges laid with respect to illegal foreign payments. It was fined $500,000. It has also been caught in military procurement controversies. It billed the Pentagon for $127,000 in political contributions. In other words, it gave money to politicians and then it billed the Pentagon for the same amount. It also sold pliers to the Pentagon for $700 a pair. That is a way of doing business, I suppose, but if the Government thinks that somehow it is going to get a different kind of treatment, it is wrong. In 1979, Boeing again cut its workforce from 155,000 to 50,000. It basically closed up its operations here. That is the difference, Mr. Speaker. It will be making those corporate decisions in Seattle and Spokane based upon the interests of its entire corporate empire and Canada, as a small division way over in the corner, will simply take what it can get.
The President of Boeing made a comment in today's Wall Street Journal. He was quoted as saying that the de Havilland line of products will represent a very small percentage of the total commercial sales of Boeing, that one 747 is equal to almost 20 of the turbo-prop products of de Havilland. Boeing certainly has a world-wide marketing network, but if you are a salesman for Boeing and you are trying to hustle a 747, a 756 or a 767, and you are spending your time and your expense account, you are going for the big product, not 20 to make up one. It is like Avon calling and you are trying to sell the person at home the full line of products and saying as an aside, "I have a little toothpaste in my bag as well".
The difference is that de Havilland is an independent Canadian company. It should have the opportunity to go out into the world market and sell our aeroplanes with pride and integrity not because we have a great line of jumbo jets but because it is our own product and we know there is a niche in the market for it and we are going out to exploit that particular part of the market. We should not be part of a great massive bazaar where we throw our wares out in front of everyone, saying: "If you buy our 747s, we will give you a
Supply
couple of Dash-8s as a bonus". An independent company would have given us our own independent marketing ability. We would have been able to go into those world markets to develop our own capacity and our own potential in those markets. That is something which 1 believe Canadians wanted. That is something which has been taken away from them by this Government.
With respect to research and development, the Government tells us it is going to have this vast capital resource of Boeing to help exploit future development. I would suggest that Hon. Members of the Conservative Party read the very long article in the business pages of The New York Times of September 8. It talks about the big responsibility and obligation of the new president of Boeing. He will have to make tough choices. He has military planes and computer hardware. He has big commercial aircraft. He does not have enough capital to finance all of these things. He has to make choices between them. Does the Government think that de Havilland is going to get preference when it is competing with 747s, new SDI star wars projects and new computer development around the world? It will get it if we give Boeing sweetheart arrangements. If DRIE starts feeding it gobs of new research grants and more loans, Boeing will say, "Oh, yes, we will take it". Of course, it will. But the point is that in terms of research and development, the Dash-8 is now a fully mature aeroplane. It is out in the market. At some point down the line we have to ask ourselves what the future is of de Havilland. What new generation of air products will begin to be developed by that company? Where is the money going to come from for that? Are we going to find, as has happened with virtually every other company which has been absorbed by this large multinational, that the engineering, the administration, the R and D and the corporate decision making, will be consolidated at the American headquarters and the de Havilland division will be just one in a long line of supplicants for a very scarce amount of resources? We will become a sub-assembly plant in Canada. That is the future.
We are losing our sense of independence to become a sub-assembly plant. That, perhaps, says it all about the economic philosophy os this Government. It is happy that Canada becomes a sub-assembly plant for the big American corporate empires. It has no sense of pride that we can do things on our own. It has no sense of motive, will or purpose in trying to achieve something which Canadians can do well, making sure they have the resources to do so.
