speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-CANADIAN AEROSPACE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to speak to the House on the motion concerning the sale of de Havilland to the private sector. I also consider it a great honour to have been reappointed as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, who played a decisive role in preparing the historic agreement that led to this privatization.
When this Government came to power a little over a year ago, we announced our intention of turning a number of state-owned enterprises over to the private sector. During the months following this announcement, management and the board of directors of the Canada Development Investment Corporation negotiated with great dedication, on our behalf, and were successful in concluding an agreement that will be very beneficial to Canada. And that is how Boeing has now become the owner of de Havilland.
It is good news for de Havilland, its employees and the entire Canadian aerospace industry.
Under its new management, the company is expected to grow until it becomes a major partner of international caliber within this extremely competitive industry. Canada has gradually carved a niche for itself on world markets. If we add Boeing's marketing and financial resources to de Havilland's world reputation for the manufacture of short range aircraft, I think we have a winning combination.
As was pointed out by my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), in privatizing de Havilland, our main objective was to revitalize Canada's role in the international aerospace industry, since a company must be strong and aggressive to win in an extremely competitive market, to expand its scope and create new jobs and attract new investment, de Havilland will now have access to Boeing's sophisticated marketing network as well as its technical expertise and financial resources. The result will be a stronger and more viable company that will safeguard existing jobs while creating the potential for new jobs across Canada. A company that provides employment is a healthy company.
We expect the agreement with Boeing to increase employment in Canada generally, as well as at the de Havilland plant in Downsview. The sale proposal provided for a purchase price
Supply
of $155 million, including $65 million in the form of a repayable note. Under the terms of our agreement, for each $5 million worth of new jobs created by Boeing, $1 million will be cut off the amount owing. This could mean new projects estimated at $325 million across Canada, and the potential for thousands of jobs across the country.
Under the new management de Havilland will be responsible for designing and making all short-range Boeing aircraft for world-wide markets, thus maintaining Canadian leadership in that technological sector of aviation. Boeing fully expects to expand its sphere of activities at Downsview's de Havilland plant so as to make better use of existing manpower and equipment. We are extremely pleased with the way the negotiations were carried out with Boeing, and with the signing of the letter of intent which was finalized by the sale announcement yesterday.
There is no doubt that Boeing is an acknowledged leader in the aerospace industry, with capital investments of $9 billion and sales of approximately $13 billion last year. Boeing has also achieved an outstanding reputation in technological development and employer-employee relations. I should think that the board and management of CDIC deserve our congratulations for their efforts which led to yesterday's announcement. A number of bids were examined by the corporation, and an exhaustive market study was commissioned. CDIC management recommended acceptance of Boeing's bid and their recommendation was endorsed by several independent investment firms. They all agree that the decision is an excellent deal for Canada and Canadian taxpayers. This sale is another fulfilled commitment of our Government to take part in the economic renewal by privatizing those Crown corporations which no longer serve the best public interests. Better still, it is a unique occasion to maintain the strength and dynamism of our aerospace industry.
Our decision to sell de Havilland to private interests will have other advantages which Members of the Opposition have deliberately chosen to ignore, intent as they are to take a negative approach whenever the Government makes an announcement. For example, some of the tax provisions included in the agreement will be of special interest to Canada's regional air carriers. Our regional air carriers-so important in a country as vast as ours, and particularly in the less densely populated regions-will be able to purchase top-of-the-line equipment at low interest rates.
In fact, the growth and development of our regional air carriers are some of the main features of the policy of this Government which ensures that all Canadians receive quality services no matter where they have elected to live in this country.
Other corporations involved in the Canadian aerospace industry will also benefit from the privatization of de Havil-

December 3, 1985
Supply
land. According to the terms of the sale, Boeing has agreed to honour all previous contracts with suppliers who will also benefit from the company's increased sale volume. That is a golden opportunity for developing new contracts and co-operating with one of the greatest aerospace corporations in the world.
Contrary to our predecessors who had presided over the take-over of de Havilland, we behaved wisely and in a business like manner. The take-over occurred under a Liberal administration, without any sort of plan to ensure the growth of the firm and the expansion of its market. On the contrary, we had very precise goals in mind when we initiated the privatization of de Havilland. The privatization, as announced yesterday, will result in a renewed market, more jobs and the establishment of a strong and dynamic aerospace industry in Canada. Benefits and spin-offs are gained immediately and will accrue for many years to come.
As a Crown corporation, de Havilland seemed to alternate between good and bad years, like on a roller coaster. The number of jobs, from a record high of 5,000 in 1981, came down to nearly half of that two years later. Thanks to a new diversified investment basis which the new administration is planning now, Boeing should create a more stable environment. We believe that de Havilland had reached a critical stage in its development, a stage which required a solid direction and diversified investments from the private sector. Boeing is offering this corporation a chance to prosper and grow.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am quite surprised by the negative reactions and criticism which a number of Hon. Members opposite have voiced following the announcement of this agreement with Boeing. Yet, ever since the acquisition of de Havilland in 1974, successive Governments had never denied their intention to sell this corporation as soon as they received a reasonable offer. Now, we have received such an offer which we have carefully studied and compared with others, and we have come to an agreement with Boeing in the best interest of both the Canadian Government and taxpayers. We see no benefit or logic in hanging on to a corporation which was a burden on the Public Treasury when we realize the advantages the Boeing corporation will be offering the de Havilland corporation by providing it with a solid financial base.
A number of Hon. Members have expressed some concern. They felt that, by privatizing the de Havilland corporation, we had failed to protect the development of the Canadian aerospace technology. Their concerns are without any foundation. The growth and profitability of the Canadian aerospace industry have been among the Government's primary concerns, and guaranties to that effect are part of the agreement.
Boeing has committed itself to maintain and enhance research and development at de Havilland's and has effectively established a long term investment plan. This is an indication
of the seriousness of the corporation regarding the future. We know that Boeing is quite impressed by de Havilland engineering and will use this asset to develop the business.
As a Crown corporation, de Havilland did have some engineering successes. However, in recent times, there have been mostly failures. In view of the decision of Boeing to grant de Havilland a world product mandate for the design, development and production of the turbo-propelled shuttle, the growth potential of the company is obvious. The purpose of privatization was to find the best possible purchaser to build on the solid foundations established by de Havilland throughout the years and to guarantee job security and the creation of new jobs, not only in Toronto, but throughout Canada.
In our opinion and that of the independent financial advisers, Boeing was the company which best met our requirements.
I profoundly disagree with those who can see no benefit in this transaction simply because the headquarters of the purchasing company are located in the United States. The tendency in the aeronautical industry favours joint international endeavours which make use of the knowledge and experience of several countries.
Moreover, there is nothing new in the association of Boeing and Canada. The company already has plants in Arnprior and Winnipeg and will no doubt continue to be a good Canadian corporate citizen. Moreover, Boeing will appoint Canadians to its board of directors and consider Canadian equity participation. In other words, the Corporation understands the need to become involved in Canadian activities and has given enough evidence that it is willing to meet these requirements, including participation in other projects, jointly with Canadian suppliers.
Finally, I would like to say something about another sector of the aerospace industry which has developed in Canada in the last few years. From discussions with the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), I understand that negotiations are now underway to sell Canadair to the private sector. In the meantime, this Corporation continues to increase its sales and improve its financial situation, showing that it can meet the challenge of international competition.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that selling de Havilland benefits all Canadians and that if we could succeed in getting as good a deal and in finding purchasers as competent for Canadair, it could also be of benefit to Canadians.
Considering both this information and the agreement which ensures the development of de Havilland, I am convinced that the Canadian aerospace industry has a great future. We shall never be content to manage a branch plant industry in Canada, but we shall continue to produce the most sophisticated of airplanes, maintaining the tradition of excellence which we have always had in Canada and of which we are rightly proud.
December 3, 1985

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last Hon. Member who spoke on behalf of the Government said that he was not an expert on the airline industry and that he did not think Opposition Members were. That is probably true. 1 do not believe that most Hon. Members of the House are experts on any particular industry which we may be investigating at a given time. However, we have a wider responsibility, that is, to look at the actions of Government, especially when its actions have the effect of costing taxpayers millions and millions of dollars.
Let us look at the way in which the deal was entered into, the tax liabilities we inherited as a result of the agreement, future tax losses as a result of it, and the fact that the Government has committed itself to a share of all development costs. The people of Canada are being committed to more costs in respect of export financing. We are curious in terms of the real assets which will be sold-the value of the land, the buildings and other assets such as machinery. We do not know that information. The fact that the Parliamentary Secretary could not answer those questions is a concern to all parliamentarians.
Earlier today, a number of members of our caucus asked the Government to ensure that Parliament had access to that information. They asked for a parliamentary committee to hold hearings on the matter prior to any final vote or final
agreement. We have not received assurances from the Government in that regard, and 1 think it is very important for them to be given.
It is not just that the Auditor General said that we as parliamentarians must do a better job looking after the public purse. It is not just that the Auditor General said that one area in which Parliament was weakest, in terms of doing that job, was that of tax expenditures. Obviously the memorandum of agreement with Boeing involves many future tax commitments to that particular company. It is not only because of those two concerns that I am participating in the debate. It is because I have a concern about the future of our entire aircraft industry.
I mentioned earlier today that I was a teenager when the previous Conservative majority Government decided to destroy the Avro Arrow program. That decision was made over 20 years ago but I believe that most Canadians who grew up in that generation still believe that that was a colossal mistake. The massive Conservative majority in the House of Commons made that decision. They were so paranoid that not only did they destroy the plans for the Avro Arrow, but they took the one prototype and cut it up into one-inch pieces. They absolutely destroyed the plans for that plane and the plane itself.
As a result of that decision we not only lost the lead that we had at that time in that area, but we lost the research and development that would have followed and the technological expertise that was in the country at the time as well as the resulting jobs. We are now importing the very types of planes which the Avro Arrow was providing us with the technology to develop in Canada.
1 am afraid that what is being done in this particular case is a shadow of what the previous Conservative majority Government did over 20 years ago. The Conservatives say that they are getting rid of de Havilland because it is costing us money. Yet, we see from the very memorandum of agreement which has been signed and the few details that they have given out that we are committing ourselves to hundreds of millions of dollars of expenditure through tax write-offs or actual cash gifts to Boeing in the future. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are not selling de Havilland to Boeing just to reduce the cost to the taxpayer because the Conservative Government is committing the taxpayers of Canada to spending hundreds of millions of dollars in the future to help Boeing. I think that certainly destroys any argument the Government makes in terms of this being a financial saving to the taxpayer.
The people who work at de Havilland were not consulted before this decision was made and neither was the Parliament of Canada. We do not have before us at this time a copy of the memorandum of agreement. We have no commitment from the Government that Parliament will hold hearings on the final agreement. That is important, not only because that final agreement could cost us hundreds of millions of dollars, and not only because we have no knowledge of what is involved in terms of tax expenditures, both of which are things the Auditor General said Parliament should know about, but, probably
December 3, 1985

even more important, Parliament must have hearings and access to the complete agreement prior to it being signed because there exists the very dangerous possibility that we will again destroy the whole aircraft construction industry in the country.
We do not need another Avro Arrow. Just because the Conservative Government has the same type of massive majority in the House of Commons does not mean that it has to make the same mistake. Instead we should have a commitment from the Government that it will not blindly follow an ideological path thinking that we must get rid of Crown corporations, that we should not put any restrictions on private corporations, and that we should not be concerned that Boeing could strip the operation of de Havilland and take the technology that we paid for out of the City of Toronto to San Francisco, Seattle, or any other operation they have in the States.
That is what we are talking about here. The Government is giving Boeing the company and saying that it will give them some money and tax benefits in the future and pay for any export financing costs and development costs for the Dash-8 even though it will now be in private hands. Yet, the Government is not putting any restrictions on. It is not asking for job guarantees or any guarantees that the technology will stay in Canada. The Government is even allowing the physical assets, aside from the land, to be taken right out of the country. That has been done before, Mr. Speaker.
This is not a small deal. It is a massive deal which will cost the taxpayers of Canada hundreds of millions of dollars, not only because we will still be giving money to Boeing, but because we will be losing money that we should be collecting in taxation. We will be paying for the future development of the Dash-8. Yet we have made no requirements of Boeing. Why is that, Mr. Speaker?
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that we realize that when the Government signed this memorandum of agreement it showed us a very bad example of what it might do in the free trade negotiations. We are speaking about a Canadian Crown corporation. There is no question that it has problems and that it is costing the Canadian taxpayers. However, it also has a product which is being made and developed in Canada and guaranteed sales of over 140 planes in the next little while. What is the Government doing? Is it saying that we should have production guarantees in the country? Is it saying that those jobs should be secure for Canadians? Is it saying that there should be some concern for what happens to the people who work in that plant? No, it is not, Mr. Speaker. It is negotiating with its eyes closed. It is giving away the shop and is not requiring any guarantees on behalf of the people who will be buying a Canadian industry.
1, as well as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) and others in the House, have negotiated before. I must say that you cannot control what the other side puts on the table. However, when you go into negotiations, whether for de Havilland or the free trade pact which the Government is so keen on having with the Americans, we have a right to know
Supply
what our side is negotiating with. After having seen what I have of this memorandum of agreement I have absolutely no faith that the Conservative Government will negotiate a good deal on behalf of Canada. It has not shown that it will keep even the shirt on our back when it goes into negotiations. It has not shown that it is concerned about Canadian content, with keeping jobs in Canada, with keeping Canadian technology in Canada, or that it even knows the financial details of what it gave away.
In response to a question from the House Leader of the New Democratic Party the Parliamentary Secretary could not say what the value of the assets were. How much is that land in downtown Toronto worth? How much is that building worth? How much is the machinery worth? If we are negotiating an agreement with someone else, we should know what the heck is the value of our own position. The Government does not know the value of its own position and it is certainly not capable of knowing it when it comes to negotiating a much more massive deal with the Americans.

Mr. Speaker, on November 19, 1985, I asked a question of the President of the Treasury Board concerning the recent Supplementary Estimates. While it was encouraging that those Estimates showed a modest increase by historical standards, 1 still find it troublesome in relation to the big job this Government has to do to get the deficit under control and to reduce the awesome size of our national debt. Many of my constituents continue to be alarmed at the size of that debt.
George Yates of Denver Crescent, and Ken Stephen of Meadowglade Crescent have mentioned this issue many times. Just today I received a letter from T. Richard Davies of Himount Drive in Willowdale to which he attached an article by J. Christopher Barron which outlines in a hard-hitting fashion the situation this Government has to deal with.
I believe we are on a collision course. Our national debt is now over $200 billion and the interest cost alone is roughly $20 billion to $22 billion a year. How long can we continue to spend $105 billion a year while collecting only approximately $71 billion? Households cannot do this. Corporations cannot do this. If you do not have the money, then bankruptcy will be the end result. I submit that Governments cannot continue in this fashion either.
We can be very proud of our social programs. Our care for our elderly is second to none in the world. Senior citizens now account for approximately 10 per cent of our population, but shortly after the turn of the century that will increase to 25 per cent. If we want to continue to give to that group the care it deserves we will have to get our spending under control. In a few decades the Canada Pension Plan will be in trouble if we do not have the money to support it. Other areas will suffer as well.
However, the recent meeting of the First Ministers in Halifax once again showed the difficult problem of coming to grips with the cost of running this country. This Government was very generous in granting a 5 per cent increase in transfer payments, an amount which is higher than inflation, yet we saw the Premiers demanding 7 per cent, almost double the rate of inflation.
Adjournment Debate
Over the last 10 years the deficit has risen from a mere $2 billion to the $34 billion to $35 billion range today. Ten years ago our national debt was $24 billion. Today it is a staggering $200 billion to $225 billion. This erodes the confidence of investors. It reduces incentives for risk-taking.
Three out of four ridings elected a Conservative Member in the last general election. They wanted a change in the direction of this country. At the top of the list of things they wanted this Government to do was to get spending under control. There are a lot of good things happening now. The Nielsen task force is tackling hundreds of programs with a view to reducing their cost. Today the sale of de Havilland has been extensively debated. This company has been draining the treasury of $50 million a year and this sale will put an end to that. There are many more measures under way. 1 would just like to underscore that we know the task we have ahead of us and we will be working with due diligence to gain the respect of Canadians and get this ever-increasing deficit off of our back. In that way we can get on with the social programs which this country will need in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whenever the Government is developing a budgetary strategy, it expects planned reductions as much as possible. For example, the 1985-86 estimates reflected its firm determination to reduce our expenditures in accordance with our November 1984 financial statement.
The implementation of those economic measures has effectively allowed us to reduce current supplementary estimates. [English]
However, we must realize that Supplementary Estimates are a vehicle for seeking funds for unforeseen requirements and for new initiatives which are not finalized at the time Main Estimates are tabled. A few of the recommendations of the ministerial task force on program review are reflected in the level of Estimates for 1985-86. Still further reductions will be reflected in the 1986-87 Main Estimates.
In response to the question of when we will see absolute declines in the Estimates, we would draw our colleagues' attention to the fact that some 25 per cent of the Government's spending is on public debt charges in order to finance the current high debt levels created by the previous Government. I would also point out that almost 40 per cent of the total budget consists of transfer payments to persons directly, and other levels of Government. These payments are, for the most part, made in accordance with legislation which has indexing and other growth components built in.
With these facts in mind it is difficult to conceive of immediate over-all year-to-year decreases in spending Estimates. The aim of the Government is to reduce the budgetary deficit by reducing the growth of expenditures relative to revenues. The Minister of Finance's latest projections, as presented earlier this month in his progress report on securing

December 3, ! 985
Adjournment Debate
economic renewal, show that budgetary revenues and program expenditures will continue to rise but will be roughly in balance by 1990-91.

Our Government's budget is a priority if we are to reduce the deficit and, consequently, we definitely intend to operate within its tax limits for the current year.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS (A) PARTICIPATION OF FRANCOPHONES HORS QUEBEC AT FRANCOPHONIE SUMMIT. (B) FRANCO-ONTARIANS- FIRST-CLASS CITIZENSHIP STATUS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 18 of this year, I raised in the House a question concerning the Francophonie Summit, which appears to be taking shape and will be held at Versailles, France, in February 1986. A number of francophone countries will be meeting to discuss the future of the francophone group, something like what is done in the Commonwealth context.
I will not mention all the problems and pitfalls this meeting seems to represent for certain people, and I asked the Prime Minister-since an agreement had been concluded with Quebec and New Brunswick had also been given the assurance it would be participating on an official basis in the discussions-if he could ensure that the francophone diaspora, and I am referring to francophones outside Quebec, in the other provinces, and especially in Ontario where there are 500,000 ... I asked him whether they too could directly participate in the discussions at this meeting.
The Prime Minister said with a great deal of empathy that he fully understood my question, and that he first wanted to explain that New Brunswick had been invited because, and I quote the Prime Minister as reported at page 8543 in Hansard'.
-because the Province of New Brunswick is officially bilingual and it is a major reason for being asked to participate on an official basis.
I realize that, and the Prime Minister went on to say:
I would think that the decision was first made because New Brunswick is officially bilingual, which unfortunately is still not the case in Ontario.
And then he said:
Still I intend to look favourably upon the proposition of my colleague.
Mr. Speaker, the question this evening is whether the Prime Minister has had time to think about my proposal and whether he has a response, because I am a little concerned about the way the media, especially, reported the exchange we had in the House. 1 could give a few examples, Mr. Speaker: "Official bilingualism first says Mulroney", in referring to Ontario participation at the Francophonie Summit. "Franco-Ontarians will not be represented at the Sommet de la francophonie", a headline in Le Devoir. "Mulroney excludes Ontario from francophone summit'', in Le Droit.

" 'Lack of official bilingualism in Ontario unfortunate'. PM" and " 'Unilingual Ontario is abnormal'. PM".

Mr. Speaker, it was my intention at the time to take a position approach and make Canadians understand there are francophones living in other provinces who like to think the federal Government speaks on their behalf. We just wanted to make sure that the Government representing us at the summit proceedings will do so in the appropriate manner and provide for the kind of presence and representation with which we could feel comfortable.
1 simply want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary whether in his reply he could, for instance, give me the assurance that the president of the Association canadienne fran^aise de I'Ontario, the ACFO, who wrote to the Prime Minister on November 12 asking him, and he makes it quite clear in his letter, and I quote:
-75 per cent of Canada's francophones live in Ontario-
If we exclude Quebec and New Brunswick, of course-
-where they form an active and thriving community. It would therefore be desirable to have a Franco-Ontarian invited to join the delegation that will be representing French Canada at this international summit.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a prefectly honest and legitimate request on the part of a group of people who are Canadians first, but who happen to speak French.
I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary if he could assure us this evening that Franco-Ontarians will not be excluded from the Francophonie Summit because their province is not officially bilingual.
This is the conclusion one can draw from newspaper headlines: because the province is not bilingual, Franco-Ontarians will be excluded from the Francophonie Summit. In my judgment, that is altogether unacceptable and saddening as a conclusion.
I know, Mr. Speaker-and I would like to explain this in the few remaining minutes-that we in Canada have a very special kind of bilingualism. New Brunswick and Canada are officially bilingual, they have two official languages, French and English.
Quebec is also bilingual, but in its own way, according to Section 133 of the Constitution which stipulates: In Quebec, you must communicate with your Canadian residents in French or in English when dealing with documents of the Legislature or documents before the courts. Therefore it is institutional bilingualism, and the same institutional bilingualism exists in Manitoba. Now then, if Quebec and New Brunswick were invited because they are "bilingual", why was Manitoba not invited since it too, according to Section 23, is

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-RECOMMENDED STIFFENING OF CRIMINAL CODE POLLUTION PENALTIES
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-RECOMMENDED STIFFENING OF CRIMINAL CODE POLLUTION PENALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Law Reform Commission of Canada recently recommended that our Criminal Code be amended to include crimes against the environment. That was a rather revolutionary recommendation on the part of that Commission because traditionally lawyers and judges, when dealing with the Criminal Code, have been very, very conservative in their suggestions and have usually taken the attitude that the Criminal Code is sacrosanct and should not be amended to include new types of crimes.
The Criminal Code was originally drafted over 100 years ago. The crimes included at that time were crimes of those days. Time has passed and things have changed, but very few new offences have ever been included in the Criminal Code. Therefore, it is rather revolutionary that the Law Reform Commission is actually recommending that new offences against the environment be included.
While it is a revolutionary idea, it is understandable that the Law Reform Commission should be recommending something like this in light of what has been happening to society in the last few years. As you know, there are now over 1,200 individual chemical substances that have been identified and are considered to be dangerous. When they escape into the air, the water or, for that matter, our food, they can cause more than a small amount of trouble. We can see the effect on the physical environment from acid rain. In addition to that, we can see impact on our own physical property when the dangerous substances result in fires and explosions. In the last week or so we have heard reports that would indicate that some of these dangerous substances may be in our processed foods. All of these things will obviously cause people great concern; cause them to want to see a real form of control over the pollutants and the people who are polluting our environment.
We have had many examples of these sorts of things in recent years, as you are well aware. It is just over one year ago that there was a great chemical escape from the Union Carbide plant in Bhopal, India, which killed upwards of 2000 people. In addition, we have recently had problems with a PCB spill in Kenora, Ontario. We have had continuing problems along the Niagara River in New York State. The chemical dumps at Love Canal, Hyde Park, S area and 102nd Street in Niagara Falls, New York, are all currently seeping toxic material down the banks of the Niagara River into the River and Lake Ontario potentially causing great problems for the four million Canadians who live around Lake Ontario. We have had problems with nuclear waste at Port Hope, Ontario, as well as many, many other problems of this sort.
The Law Reform Commission has, therefore, suggested that in order to focus on this and to put some teeth in the laws we should actually include offences against the environment in our Criminal Code. They do not suggest that we should do away with all the other offences in the provincial statutes or

December 3, 1985
Adjournment Debate
other federal statutes, but do suggest that we should provide something specific in the Criminal Code to take into account serious acts of commission and omission, to take into account harmful acts, and to take into account acts which are performed with intent, wrecklessly, and with gross negligence. Those are the types of crimes against the environment that it is suggested should be included in the Criminal Code.
The commission indicates that in addition to the fines which we have now there should be penalties, orders for restitution, and jail terms for executives and directors of the polluting companies. This is not revolutionary because many other countries include this sort of thing in their laws. Ten states in the United States include this sort of thing in their laws, and West Germany and Japan both have provisions for crimes against the environment in their Criminal Codes. It is only logical that we should take this step in our country.
On November 27 I asked the Parliamentary Secretary if the Minister agreed with these recommendations and would urge the Government to amend the Criminal Code accordingly. He indicated to me that they were currently studying the matter and woulds be looking at some recommendations in the future. I hope that tonight we will hear from the Parliamentary Secretary what changes the Government is looking at. Hopefully it will be considering changes to the Criminal Code, rather than only changes to the Environmental Contaminants Act, which I know the Department has in mind. We should be making some changes to the Environmental Contaminants Act, but we should also include these very serious offences in the Criminal Code to show the people of the country that the Government is serious and wants to get on with dealing with environmental crimes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-RECOMMENDED STIFFENING OF CRIMINAL CODE POLLUTION PENALTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as an engineer and a Member of this House, I am pleased to speak about this question which relates to the reform of Canadian legislation on crimes against the environment.

I wish to inform the House that Environment Canada is now giving careful attention to the Law Reform Commission's recently released working paper on crimes against the environment. As our hon. colleague is undoubtedly aware, the working paper is a discussion document. Its tentative recommendations are intended to bring responses from various sectors, including other federal Departments. During the comment period, Environment Canada will be preparing its observations in response to the report of the Law Reform Commission.
On the international level, Canada has treaty obligations with its neighbours. One example of such an obligation is the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909, signed by Canada and the United States under which both countries are obligated to not pollute boundary and trans-boundary waters. It is this treaty which led directly to the Canada-United States Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. As well, Canada is a signatory to several international Conventions designed to protect the environment, such as the London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by the dumping of wastes and other matter at sea and the Law of the Sea Convention. All Canada's international obligations and responsibilities would therefore have to be considered before a decision could be taken to amend the Criminal Code as contemplated by the Law Reform Commission.
There are five different levels of potential environmental rights discussed by the Law Reform Commission to which Environment Canada has turned its attention. First, there is the right not to have one's life or health harmed or endangered as a result of environmental pollution. The second is the right to a reasonable level of environmental quality, even when a specific pollutant or pollution source cannot be identified with certainly to be the cause of a specific health damage or risk. The third is the right to a reasonable level of environmental quality, a quality which is violated by pollution that deprives people of the use and enjoyment of the environment even when there are no health effects or dangers.

As you can see, Mr. Speaker, we cannot agree on this complex project before scrutinizing the many aspects of the problem and the intricate considerations of an issue which has international connotations.
